Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 1, verse 1 (part 1 of 6):

[p. 39]
﴿In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾

There are several discussions here.

(First discussion) The scholars differed over whether this (the basmalah) is among the special features of this community (the Muslim ummah) or not. The allamah Abu Bakr al-Tunisi reported the consensus (ijma') of the scholars of every religion that God Most High opened every scripture with it. al-Suyuti related, in what al-Sirmini reported from him, and the responsibility for it lies with him: "In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful, is the opening of every book." This narrator (al-Sirmini) held that the basmalah is among the special features, on the basis of what is reported: "The Prophet (ﷺ) used to write: 'In Your name, O God,' until there was revealed: ﴿In the name of God is its course﴾, so he commanded that 'In the name of God' be written, until there was revealed: ﴿Say: Call upon God or call upon the Most Gracious﴾, so he commanded that 'In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful' be written, until the verse of al-Naml was revealed, and he commanded that 'In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful' be written." It is also well known that the meanings of the books are in the Qur'an, its meanings are in al-Fatihah, its meanings are in the basmalah, and the meanings of the basmalah are in the letter ba'. Had it been in the earlier books, he would have been commanded from the outset to write it, and the meanings of the Qur'an would have been in every book; the consequent is false, so the antecedent is too. But it may be objected that the command to write it in that detail does not entail a denial, since it is possible that knowledge of it was absent at that time, and there is no harm in that. Moreover, what is exclusive to the Qur'an is the Arabic wording in this order; the scriptures as a whole, contrary to al-Ghaytі, are not in Arabic, and what the Qur'an contains of them is translated. Therefore these words may well have a role in comprising all the meanings, so they are not in other than the Qur'an, as al-Sirmini supposed, even if there is a basmalah there. Furthermore, the apparent sense of the first of the two proofs itself indicates that it is not exclusive.

(Second discussion) This is one of the fundamental questions, to the extent that a group devoted a separate work to it. People differed over the basmalah outside Surah al-Naml, since it is by agreement part of a verse there, on ten opinions:

(1) It is not a verse of the surahs at all.
(2) It is a verse of all surahs except Bara'ah (al-Tawbah).
(3) It is a verse of al-Fatihah only, and not of others.
(4) It is part of a verse of them only.
(5) It is a single verse, revealed to indicate the beginnings of surahs for blessing and to separate them from one another.
(6) It is permissible to make it a verse of them and not a verse, since it was revealed repeatedly in both descriptions.
(7) It is part of a verse of all surahs.
(8) It is a verse of al-Fatihah and part of a verse of the (other) surahs.
(9) The reverse of that.
(10) It is separate verses; though it was revealed many times. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn al-Mubarak, the people of Mecca such as Ibn Kathir, the people of Kufa such as 'Asim and al-Kisa'i and others, except Hamzah, and most of the companions of al-Shafi'i and the Imamiyyah, according to the second opinion. Some of the Shafi'is and Hamzah said the third, and it is attributed to Imam Ahmad. The people of Medina, including Malik, the people of Syria, including al-Awza'i, and the people of Basra, including Abu 'Amr and Ya'qub, held the fifth, which is the well-known position of our school (the Hanafi school). A person must support his school, defend it, and establish proofs for its affirmation and weaken the arguments of its opponents. I used to count the noble Shafi'i scholars as my party and reckoned myself among them alone, and the brilliance of their statements had captured my heart, just as Layla al-Amiriyyah captured the heart of Qays. Wherever it shone, I had no precedence or lag concerning it:

Her love came to me before I knew love, and it met an empty heart and settled there.

Until what happened happened, and I became occupied with the statements of the noble Hanafi scholars, and I dwelt in the gardens of the anemones of al-Nu'man, and her love so possessed me that I began to hum the words of the poet:

Her love erased the love of those who were before her, and settled in a place that had not been settled before.

Al-Fakhr (al-Razi) has indeed prolonged the discussion in this place, and he set out sixteen proofs that it is a verse of al-Fatihah, as the text of his words shows. But there is no value in the translation (of that). Behold, by God's grace I shall refute it, and there is no boasting, and I shall support my school by God's support, and from Him comes support and victory. So I say:

[p. 40]
(First proof) al-Shafi'i related from Ibn Juraij, from Abu Mulaykah, from Umm Salamah that she said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) recited the Opening of the Book, and he counted: ﴿In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾ as a verse; ﴿Praise be to God, Lord of the worlds﴾ as a verse; ﴿The Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾ as a verse; ﴿Master of the Day of Judgement﴾ as a verse; ﴿You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help﴾ as a verse; ﴿Guide us to the straight path﴾ as a verse; ﴿The path of those You have blessed, not of those who have earned Your anger, nor of those who are astray﴾ as a verse." This is an explicit text.

(Second proof) Sa'id al-Maqburi related from his father, from Abu Hurayrah, that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "The Opening of the Book is seven verses, the first of which is: ﴿In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾."

(Third proof) al-Tha'labi related with his chain from Abu Burdah, from his father, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Shall I inform you of a verse that has not been revealed to anyone after Sulayman ibn Dawud except me?" I said: "Yes." He said: "With what do you begin the Qur'an when you open the prayer?" I said: "In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful." He said: "It is it."

(Fourth proof) al-Tha'labi related with his chain from Ja'far ibn Muhammad, from his father, "from Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said to him: 'How do you say when you stand for prayer?' He said: 'I say: ﴿Praise be to God, Lord of the worlds﴾.' He said: 'Say: ﴿In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾.'" He also related with his chain from Umm Salamah "that the Prophet (ﷺ) used to recite: ﴿In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾ ﴿Praise be to God, Lord of the worlds﴾." He also related with his chain from 'Ali, may God honour his face, that when he began a surah in prayer he would recite: "In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful," and he would say: "Whoever leaves its recitation has diminished." He also related with his chain from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn 'Abbas, concerning the words of God Most High: ﴿And We have certainly given you seven of the oft-repeated and the magnificent Qur'an﴾, that he said: "The Opening of the Book." It was said to Ibn 'Abbas: "Then where is the seventh?" He said: "In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful." And with his chain, from Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "When you recite the Mother of the Qur'an, do not omit: 'In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful,' for it is one of its verses." And also with his chain, from Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: God, Mighty and Majestic, says: "I have divided the prayer between Me and My servant into two halves. When he says: ﴿In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾, God Most High says: 'My servant has glorified Me.' When he says: ﴿Praise be to God, Lord of the worlds﴾, God says: 'My servant has praised Me.' When he says: ﴿The Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾, he says: 'My servant has extolled Me.' When he says: ﴿Master of the Day of Judgement﴾, God Most High says: 'My servant has entrusted himself to Me.' When he says: ﴿You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help﴾, God Most High says: 'This is between Me and My servant.' When he says: ﴿Guide us to the straight path﴾, God Most High says: 'This is for My servant, and for My servant is what he asks.'" And also with his chain, from Abu Hurayrah, who said: "I was with the Prophet (ﷺ) in the mosque, and the Prophet was speaking to his companions, when a man entered and prayed, opened the prayer, sought refuge, and then said: ﴿Praise be to God, Lord of the worlds﴾. The Prophet (ﷺ) heard that and said to him: 'O man, you have cut your prayer short for yourself. Do you not know that ﴿In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾ is part of the praise? Whoever leaves it has left out a verse of it, and whoever leaves out a verse of it has cut short his prayer, for there is no prayer except with it; whoever leaves out a verse of it has nullified his prayer.'" And with his chain from Talhah ibn 'Ubayd Allah, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Whoever leaves out ﴿In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾ has left out a verse from the Book of God."

(Fifth proof) The recitation of ﴿In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾ is obligatory at the beginning of al-Fatihah, and if that is so, it must be a verse of it. (The proof of the first premise): ﴿Read in the name of your Lord﴾. It is not permissible to say that the ba' is superfluous (sila), because the principle is that every letter of the speech of God Most High has a purpose, and if the letter is meaningful, the sense is: "Read, beginning in the name of your Lord." The apparent sense of a command is obligation, and it has not been established outside recitation for the prayer; therefore it must be established in recitation within the prayer, to preserve the text from being rendered inoperative.

(Sixth proof) The basmalah is written in the script of the Qur'an, and whatever is not of the Qur'an is not written in the script of the Qur'an. Do you not see that they forbade writing the names of the surahs in the codex, and forbade the markings for tens and fifths?

[p. 41]
The purpose of all that is to prevent what is not Qur'an from being mixed with the Qur'an. Had the basmalah not been of the Qur'an, they would not have written it in the script of the Qur'an.

(Seventh proof) The Muslims agreed that what lies between the two covers is the speech of God Most High, and the basmalah exists between them, so it must be counted as part of it.

(Eighth proof) The majority agreed that al-Fatihah is seven verses, except that al-Shafi'i said: "In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful, is a verse," and Abu Hanifah said: "It is not a verse, but ﴿The path of those You have blessed﴾ is a verse." We shall show that his view is weak and feeble. Then it remains that the verses cannot be seven unless the basmalah is counted as a complete verse of it.

(Ninth proof) We say: The recitation of the basmalah before al-Fatihah is obligatory, so it must be a verse of it. The proof of the first premise: Abu Hanifah concedes that its recitation is more excellent. If that is so, the apparent sense is that the Prophet (may God bless him, his family and grant them peace) recited it, so it becomes obligatory for us to recite it, by the words of God Most High: ﴿Follow him﴾. If its obligation is established, it is established that it is part of the surah, because there is no one who makes a distinction. Also the words of the Prayer and Peace be upon him: "Every matter of importance that does not begin with the name of God is cut off (abtar)." And the greatest of deeds after faith is the prayer, so reciting al-Fatihah without reciting the basmalah makes the prayer an "abtar" deed, and the word indicates the utmost deficiency and defect, as is shown by the fact that it was used as a reproach to the disbelieving hater (al-shani'). So it must be said that a prayer empty of it is in utmost deficiency and defect, and whoever admits this speaks of invalidity, and this indicates that it is part of al-Fatihah.

(Tenth proof) What is reported: "The Prophet (ﷺ) said to Ubayy ibn Ka'b: 'What is the greatest verse in the Qur'an?' He said: 'In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.'" The Prophet confirmed his statement. The basis of the inference is that this shows this amount is a complete verse; and it is known that it is not a complete verse in al-Naml, so it must be so in other surahs, and there is nothing but al-Fatihah.

(Eleventh proof) From Anas: Mu'awiyah came to Medina and led the people in a loud prayer, and he recited the Mother of the Qur'an without reciting the basmalah. When he finished his prayer, the Muhajirun and the Ansar called out to him from every side: "Have you forgotten? Where is ﴿In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾ when you began the Qur'an?" So Mu'awiyah repeated the prayer and recited it aloud.

(Twelfth proof) All the prophets, at the beginning of their good works, began with the name of God. Noah said: ﴿In the name of God is its course﴾, and Sulayman: ﴿In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. Do not exalt yourselves over me﴾. So it must be obligatory for our Prophet too, by His words: ﴿So follow their guidance﴾. If that is established for him, it is established for us too, by His words: "Follow him." And if it is established for us, it is established that it is a verse of the surah of al-Fatihah.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 1, verse 1 (part 2 of 6):**

(The Thirteenth Argument) He, exalted is He, is eternal, and what is other than Him is originated. Therefore, by the rule of rational correspondence, His mention must precede the mention of anything else. Precedence in mention is achieved only if the recitation of the basmala comes first. Since it is established that the claim of the obligation of this precedence holds, then "whatever the believers deem good is good in the sight of Allah." And since the obligation of the recitation is established, it is established that it is a verse of al-Fatiha, because there is no one who distinguishes between them.

(The Fourteenth Argument) There is no doubt that it is part of the Qur'an in Surah al-Naml. Moreover, we see it repeated in the script of the Qur'an. Therefore, it must be part of the Qur'an, just as we have seen the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Woe that Day to the deniers﴾ and ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord would you deny?﴾ repeated in the same way. We say: all of it is from Him.

(The Fifteenth Argument) It has been narrated that "he (peace be upon him) used to write: *Bismika Allahumma* (In Your name, O Allah)," the hadith... and it indicates that all the parts of this phrase are from the Qur'an, and their collective whole is from it, and it is recorded in it. Therefore, it is necessary to affirm with certainty that it is from the Qur'an. For if it were permissible to exclude it despite these requirements and this widespread recognition, then the permissibility of excluding the rest of the verses would be more appropriate, and that would entail a challenge to the Mighty Qur'an.

(The Sixteenth Argument) We have already shown that it is established by *tawatur* (mass transmission) that Allah, the Exalted, used to send down this phrase upon Muhammad, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, and that he (peace be upon him) would command its writing in the script of the *mushaf* (Qur'an codex). We have also shown that the essence of the disagreement is whether its recitation is obligatory, and whether it is permissible for one in a state of ritual impurity (*muhdith*) to touch it. We say: the establishing of these rulings is more cautious, so it is necessary to adopt it, based on the saying of the Prophet, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him: "Leave what makes you doubtful for what does not make you doubtful."

The words of this scholar have ended, and it is nothing (of substance). This is because part of it has an answer, and part of it does not constitute a proof against us. The correct position of our school is that *Bismillah al-Rahman al-Rahim* is an independent verse, and it is from the Qur'an, even if it is not from al-Fatiha itself. Many of us have made its recitation obligatory in prayer. Al-Zayla'i, in his commentary on *al-Kanz*, mentioned that the more correct view is that it is obligatory. Al-Zahidi, citing *al-Mujtaba*, mentioned that the correct view is that it is
[Page 42]
obligatory in every rak'ah in which recitation is obligatory. This is the sound narration from Abu Hanifah, may Allah be pleased with him. Ibn Wahban said in his poetic work:

"If one forgets to say the basmala in every rak'ah, / he must perform the prostration of forgetfulness, according to the majority who hold it obligatory."

In *Ghunyat al-Mutamalli*: "This is the more cautious view, and with it I say, in contrast to Qadi Khan, the author of *al-Khulasa*, and others. The truth deserves to be followed." The statement attributed to some of them that this is a slip of the pen is an extreme slip, and an extreme form of partisanship without precision.

Let us discuss what this scholar mentioned in detail. As for what he mentioned in the First Argument, from the hadith of Umm Salamah in the form he narrated, which differs from what is in al-Baydawi, and which differs from what is in the hadith books: it is answered that Abu Mulaykah's hearing from Umm Salamah has not been established. Even assuming contemporaneity, it is said that this wording is not found in the well-known versions, and perhaps he (al-Baydawi) transmitted it by meaning, according to what appeared to him, in reference to some of the following narrations. Abu 'Ubayd, Ahmad, and Abu Dawud recorded with the wording: "The Messenger of Allah, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, used to pause in his recitation verse by verse: ﴿In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾, ﴿All praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾, ﴿the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾, ﴿Master of the Day of Judgment﴾." Ibn al-Anbari and al-Bayhaqi (narrated): "When he recited, he would divide his recitation verse by verse, saying: ﴿In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾, then he would pause; then he would say: ﴿All praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾, then he would pause; then he would say: ﴿the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾, then he would pause; then he would say: ﴿Master of the Day of Judgment﴾." Ibn Khuzaymah and al-Hakim (narrated) with the wording: "That the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, recited in the prayer: ﴿In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾, counting it as a verse; ﴿All praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾ as two; ﴿the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾ as three verses; ﴿Master of the Day of Judgment﴾ as four verses. And he said: 'Thus,' ﴿You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help﴾, and he gathered his five fingers." Al-Daraqutni (narrated) with the wording: "He used to recite: ﴿In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾, ﴿All praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾ until its end; he divided it verse by verse and counted it as the Bedouins count, and he counted ﴿In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾, but he did not count ﴿upon whom﴾."

The first and second narrations can be said to refer to the explanation of how the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, recited the rest of the Qur'an, and mention some of it by way of example, without exhausting it. Nothing in them indicates anything beyond establishing that it is a verse, which we concede, but from the Qur'an; as for whether it is from al-Fatiha, no. Similarly, the third narration establishes that he (peace be upon him) used to recite it in prayer and count it as a verse, because he would pause upon it. This is also conceded by us. It is the first verse of the Qur'an, and the second verse is ﴿All praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾, and so on until the fifth, and he gathered his fingers, and the speech ended.

As for the fourth narration, it is also not explicit that the basmala is a verse of al-Fatiha, for it is possible that the meaning is: he (peace be upon him) used to recite at some times in the prayer or otherwise, and not constantly, neither by convention nor by usage from the Book of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾, ﴿All praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾ until its end, that is, the verses, he divided them verse by verse, and did not connect some of them with others, and he counted them as the Bedouins count, one by one, and he counted ﴿In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾ and did not omit it, due to its obligation in prayer, and out of care for it outside of prayer, because of the great secrets and subtle thoughts it contains. For this reason, many of our scholars made the prostration of forgetfulness obligatory upon one who omits it. The Prophet, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, by this removed the suspicion that it is not part of the Qur'an, since it is used at the beginnings of letters and the starts of matters. He did not count ﴿the path of those upon whom You have bestowed favour﴾ and did not pause upon it, but he joined it (to the previous one) that time, to show permissibility and that nothing imagined contradicts its being a verse. Rather, there is something that suggests this, for the closeness of verses in length and shortness is like the closeness of rhymed units, which is desirable, and the lack of similarity in the endings does not harm. How many groups of the Conquest (Surah al-Fath)... Thus the obligation of maintaining the rhyme is not necessary. The subject being in one verse and its attribute in another verse is preceded by the example and precedes the examples. Whoever Allah has blessed, and who knows those upon whom ﴿You have bestowed favour﴾, finds it complete, and considers its dependence on the implied condition of "other than those who earned anger" to be an incomplete statement. In light of this, the narration establishes nothing beyond the basmala being a verse of the Qur'an, and this is conceded by both parties. As for whether it is from al-Fatiha, it is far beyond reach (lit. "like scraping thorns with the hand").

As for what he mentioned in the Second Argument, from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, it was recorded by al-Tabarani, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi with the wording: "﴿All praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾ are seven verses, and ﴿In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾ is one of them. They are the seven oft-repeated (*al-sab' al-mathani*) and the Great Qur'an, and it is the Mother of the Qur'an, and it is the Opening of the Book." Al-Daraqutni recorded it with the wording: "When you recite the Praise, recite ﴿In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾, for it is the Mother of the Qur'an and the Mother of the Book, and the seven oft-repeated, and ﴿In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾ is one of its verses."

The meaning of the first narration is: ﴿All praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾ up to the end of the verses are seven verses, and the Hanafis hold this view. When the Prophet, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, noticed the listeners' suspicion, arising from his not mentioning the basmala together with the previous doubt that it is not a verse of the Qur'an, he removed this suspicion in an eloquent way, saying: ﴿In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾ is one of them, that is, like one of them in being a verse of the Qur'an. The meaning of the second: when you intend to recite the Praise up to the end of what follows, recite before it ﴿In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾; it, that is, the Praise up to the end, is the Mother of the Qur'an, the Mother of the Book, and the seven oft-repeated. This is like a reason or an encouragement to recite ﴿All praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾ until its end. And his saying: "and ﴿In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾ is one of its verses" is in the same manner as what was mentioned in the meaning of the first narration. It too is like a reason or an encouragement to recite the basmala. What we have mentioned, although it involves some use of metaphor, was required by keeping the beginning of the statement on its literal meaning. If this is applied to its apparent sense, then it is necessary to use metaphor at the beginning, as is not hidden, and that is a departure from the principle without need for it.

As for what he mentioned in the Third Argument, it is nothing but establishing that the naming (basmala) is from the Qur'an, as he himself acknowledged, and we are not among those who oppose him in this.

As for what he mentioned in the Fourth, the first, second, third, sixth (despite its weakness), and eighth narrations do not indicate the intended point, and we say what they indicate. The fourth is attributed (mawquf) to Ibn 'Abbas, and we do not concede that its ruling is elevated (marfu') to the Prophet, because of the permissibility of *ijtihad* (independent reasoning), even if we say that the correct view is that a verse is known only through a revelatory determination (*tawqif*) from the Lawgiver, like knowing the surah, for example. That is why they counted "Alif Lam Mim" as a verse wherever it occurs, but did not count "Alif Lam Mim Ra" as one. This is because we have not said that it is part of a verse, and he made *ijtihad* and made it a verse; rather, we said that it is an independent verse of the Qur'an, and he made *ijtihad* and made it a verse of al-Fatiha. Or we say: he also said that on the basis of *tawqif*, but on his own assumption and *ijtihad* that it was *tawqif*.

As for the fifth, I have doubt about its authenticity in this wording. Perhaps it is in the wording by which al-Daraqutni transmitted it, and it has already passed with its explanation. I do not rely on al-Fakhr (al-Razi) regarding the hadiths, as he was not among their memorizers, and I suspect that when he transmits by meaning he alters it. I do not have al-Tha'labi's tafsir in front of me to verify this, for the transmission is from it. The seventh does not show the beauty of the speech of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, nor his eloquence, and he is the most eloquent of those who spoke the *dad* (Arabic letter). Rather, whoever has examined the hadiths has decided that this is fabricated. By my life, if it were authentic, the Shafi'is would have relied on it alone or would have given it precedence over all their other evidences. Would that he had mentioned its chain of transmission so that we might see it.

As for the Fifth Argument, we do not concede that its obligation at the beginning of al-Fatiha entails that it is a verse of it. His use of the verse ﴿Recite in the name of your Lord﴾ in this context is extremely weak for reasons clearer than the sun, so we will not weary the fingers with explaining them.

As for the Sixth Argument, it is the strongest argument used to prove that the basmala is from the Qur'an, but as for proving that it is from al-Fatiha, no. Those who deny that it is Qur'an have engaged in discussing this evidence in a way that a sound nature and a straight mind would not approve. Fairness is half of religion, and submission to the truth is among the characteristics of believers.

As for the Seventh Argument, it is in our favour, not against us, as is not hidden.

As for the Eighth Argument, apart from establishing its basis, which is the weakening of the words of our master Abu Hanifah, may Allah have mercy on him, it is like firm mountains.

As for the Ninth Argument, it is exactly like the Fifth Argument, step by step. His use of the statement "every matter of importance (*dhi bal*)" etc. is nothing, because al-Fatiha is part of the prayer, which begins with the *takbir* (saying Allahu Akbar) coinciding with the intention, which is a pillar of it. Therefore, when it is not begun with the basmala, it is considered "truncated" (*batra'*) and so is invalid. Likewise, bowing and prostration, in which the servant is closest to his Lord, each of these is a matter of importance; so when it is not begun with the basmala, it is "severed" (*abtar*) and invalid. So the good opinion of the scholar's piety and knowledge is that he used to say the basmala at the start...

his prayer, and at his bowing, his prostration, and all his other movements, may the mercy of Allah the Exalted be upon him. As for the tenth argument, it does not stand against us, because we have already informed you of our school. As for the eleventh argument, the most it indicates, even if we concede it, is that when Mu'awiyah did not recite the basmalah, he omitted an obligatory element and did not perform the prostration of forgetfulness (sujud al-sahw), so he repeated the prayer in order for it to be performed free of defect. For this reason they gave him time until he finished, so that they could see whether the defect is compensated by the prostration of forgetfulness or not. Their objection to him for omitting an obligatory element that is compensated by prostration is no stranger than their objection to him in that same prayer for omitting a recommended form (hay'ah). For al-Shafi'i himself narrated, as al-Fakhr himself transmitted, that Mu'awiyah came to Medina, led them in prayer, did not recite ﴿In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾, and did not say the takbir when lowering into bowing and prostration. When he finished the prayer, the Muhajirun and the Ansar called out to him: "O Mu'awiyah, you have stolen from the prayer! Where is ﴿In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾ and where is the takbir at bowing and prostration?" Then he repeated the prayer with the basmalah and the takbir. This does not harm us. Yes, the matter of audible recitation remains, and the discussion of it is now hidden. As for the twelfth argument, as has been mentioned before, it contains that obligation does not necessitate being a part (of the surah). Moreover, his statement: "All the prophets begin the undertaking of good deeds with the remembrance of Allah, so it was obligatory upon our Prophet to do the same, etc.," and his deduction of the obligation for him from their obligation upon them, peace be upon them, from the words of the Exalted: ﴿Those are the ones whom Allah guided, so follow their guidance﴾, I do not know what to say about it except that it is ignorance of tafsir (exegesis) and a lack of familiarity with the reports of the Bearer of Good News and the Warner. As for the thirteenth argument, it will not benefit him in opposing us either, and it has what its sister arguments have. As for the remaining arguments, they are like many of the earlier ones; they will not benefit in debate with us except by blackening paper and wasting precious breaths. Furthermore, some of what he mentioned is opposed by what Muslim and others transmitted from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: Allah the Exalted said: "I have divided the prayer between Myself and My servant into two halves, and My servant shall have what he asks. When the servant says: ﴿All praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾, Allah the Exalted says: My servant has praised Me. When he says: ﴿The Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾, He says: My servant has extolled Me. When he says: ﴿Master of the Day of Judgment﴾, He says: My servant has glorified Me. When he says: ﴿You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help﴾, He says: This is between Me and My servant, and My servant shall have what he asks. When he says: ﴿Guide us to the straight path, the path of those upon whom You have bestowed favor, not of those who have earned anger, nor of those who are astray﴾, He says: This is for My servant, and My servant shall have what he asks." This indicates that the basmalah is not part of al-Fatihah, and that it (the surah) is seven verses without it, since He made the middle ﴿You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help﴾ and the three before it for Allah the Exalted, and the three after it for the servant. There is no denial in it that the basmalah is part of the Qur'an. Without doubt this narration is more authentic than the narration of al-Tha'labi, and I do not prefer al-Tha'labi over Muslim. Likewise (it is more authentic) than the narration of al-Sijistani. Whenever a trustworthy narrator contradicts one who is more trustworthy than him by adding or omitting something, his report is shadhdh (anomalous). This is not a matter of negation and affirmation, as he who lacks firm grounding and stability in this field supposed. Interpreting "half" here as half in meaning or in kind is a lack of fairness, since that would be a metaphor, and there is no need for it nor any indicator for it. Taking it as a literal meaning but in terms of supplication and praise is refuted by counting and by the statement that the basis of the narration is al-'Ala', whom Ibn Ma'in declared weak. So, despite the man's eminence, he neither fattens nor satisfies from hunger, because those who vouch for his reliability are many. Giving precedence to disparagement (jarh) over vouching (ta'dil) is not absolute; it applies only if the vouchers are not very numerous, and here they are numerous. And that the division concerns what pertains to al-Fatihah and the basmalah jointly, together with it being contrary to the apparent meaning, is not required by wisdom, since according to the opponent it is the most noble of the parts. And that the intended meaning is a portion of the recitation of the prayer, since the apparent meaning cannot be intended because of the presence of the actions, and the joining of the surah, and a portion being realized by this portion, is nothing, since it is proper that a portion be independent with a beginning and an end, and the second (portion) exists, while the first is according to our view. Furthermore, al-Fatihah is a surah like al-Kawthar and al-Mulk. The Prophet (ﷺ) explicitly stated, in what Abu Hurayrah narrated from him, that the first (surah) has three verses, and the second has thirty, and he showed them (the Companions) that, and he did not count the basmalah. Had he counted it as a separate verse, he would have increased the count, or as a part, it would have been reported. The one who affirms it must provide proof, and how could he? Furthermore, the second (view) entails arbitrariness in asserting independence in al-Fatihah and being a part in other surahs. And al-Razi's statement is not far-fetched: ﴿All praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾ is at times a verse and at other times part of another verse, as in ﴿and the last of their call﴾, the verse, is far-fetched, indeed it is a false analogy, because the cause of being a part exists there and is absent here. Furthermore, many surahs were revealed without the basmalah, and it was then added afterward. The sound hadith on the beginning of revelation indicates the correctness of what we have said. This makes it unlikely that it is a verse of the surah or a part of a verse. And the fact that it had not yet been revealed makes the second (view) unlikely, if it does not make the first unlikely. The hadith that it was the first thing revealed is not strong; rather it is established, and what is reported poses a difficulty for it: that he used to write "In Your name, O Allah," etc. Moreover, if the priority is accepted and granted, it does not harm us. In sum, the belief that the basmalah is not a part of a surah is almost among the matters of natural disposition (fitriyyat), as is not hidden from one whose sound intuition is intact. So it is a verse of the Qur'an, independent. One who has examined the hadiths should not hesitate about its Qur'anic status, nor deny the obligation of reciting it, nor say that it is merely a sunnah. By Allah, even if the earth were filled for me with gold, I would not adopt this view, even if I could find an acceptable interpretation of it (and the favor is from Allah the Exalted). How could I, when the books of hadith are full of what indicates the opposite? This is the view that is authentically established for me from the Imam. The claim that he did not state anything (explicitly) is nothing. How could he not state it throughout his life on such a grave matter, upon which depends the question of the prayer's validity or completeness, and upon which some of the legal rulings and religious matters can be based, such as divorce, oaths, and conditional clauses? He is the greatest Imam and the earliest mujtahid, may Allah the Exalted be pleased with him. Reciting it silently in audibly recited prayers does not indicate that it is merely a sunnah, for holding that it is obligatory does not contradict silent recitation, in following the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Thus from Ibn Abbas: "The Prophet (ﷺ) did not recite the basmalah audibly until he died." And Muslim narrated from Anas: "I prayed behind the Prophet (ﷺ), Abu Bakr, Umar, and Uthman, and I did not hear any of them reciting: 'In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.'" It does not report the denial of recitation, but rather the hearing of it, in the sense of silent recitation, as is evidenced by what is explicitly stated from him: that they did not recite audibly "In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful." This was narrated by Ahmad and al-Nasa'i with a chain meeting the conditions of al-Shaykhayn (Bukhari and Muslim). Al-Tabarani narrated with a chain from him: "that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to recite the basmalah silently, and Abu Bakr, Umar, Uthman, and Ali, may Allah be pleased with them." It was also narrated from Abd Allah ibn al-Mughaffal, and we do not accept its weakness, that he said: "My father heard me saying: 'In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful,' and he said: 'O my son, beware of innovation in Islam. I prayed behind the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), behind Abu Bakr, Umar, and Uthman, and they began the recitation with ﴿All praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾. So when you pray, say: ﴿All praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾.'" That is, recite it audibly and recite the basmalah silently. This is the view of al-Thawri, Ibn al-Mubarak, Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn al-Zubayr, Ammar ibn Yasir, al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Husayn, al-Sha'bi, al-Nakha'i, Qatadah, Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz, al-A'mash, al-Zuhri, Mujahid, Ahmad, and a great many others. As for the hadiths of audible recitation, none of them is authentic except the hadith of Ibn Abbas narrated by al-Shafi'i from him: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to recite audibly: 'In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.'" This is contradicted by what was mentioned earlier from him, or it is interpreted as meaning that he recited it audibly at times to show that it is to be recited in the prayer, just as Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, recited the praise audibly for instruction, and just as the takbir was legislated to be audible for announcement. And "until he died" qualifies the negated, not the negation, so they do not contradict each other. Furthermore, it is reported from some of the memorizers of hadith that there is no explicit hadith on audible recitation without some criticism in its chain. And from al-Daraqutni: he composed a book on audible recitation, and some of the Malikis adjured him to inform them of the authentic (report), so he said: "No authentic hadith on audible recitation has been established." The claim that the reports from Anas are six and contradictory, so at times audible recitation is reported from him and at other times silent recitation, out of fear of the Banu Umayyah who opposed Ali, may Allah honor his face, since his school is audible recitation, does not harm us. For in cases of contradiction, the report with the stronger chain is given precedence, and here it is what agrees with us, since it meets the conditions of al-Shaykhayn. And the accusation of lying against Anas by the opposing narrator is, in my view, less serious than the accusation against Anas, the companion of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), of lying about the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and the foremost of his companions.

* * *

(Among the wonders of al-Razi) how he puts forward the possibility of accusation, and reports the objection of the people of Medina against the lord of the kings of the Banu Umayyah with that vile expression and that lofty position. Why did they not fear and remain silent and make peace? And more astonishing than this is that he mentioned six arguments for proving audible recitation, which are more obscure than their absence. (First) that the basmalah is part of the surah, so its ruling is the same as the surah's, silent or audible. That some of it is silent and some audible is inconsistent, and what you have learned in the refutations refutes it. And even granting that it is part of the surah, what prevents part of it from being silent and part audible? The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) did so, and "follow him." Perhaps the secret in this is like the secret in silent and audible recitation within the rak'ahs of a single prayer. Or it may be said: the state of the one upon whom the Qur'an was revealed was at first in seclusion and then in openness, and his state corresponded to its state. Indeed, if you reflect on the words of the Exalted in the sacred hadith, which is established among the people of Allah: "I was a hidden treasure," etc., a greater secret will become apparent to you. May Allah be pleased with the earliest mujtahid. (Second) that it is praise and glorification, so it is obligatory to proclaim it, based on the words of the Exalted: ﴿Remember Allah as you remember your fathers, or with even greater remembrance﴾. This is refuted by the fact that most of the contents of the prayer are like that, so should they be recited audibly? (Third) that audibly mentioning Allah indicates pride in Him and indifference to His denier, and this is rationally commendable, so it is likewise legally commendable. Nothing is hidden except what contains a defect. Then he said: "This argument is strong in my soul, firmly rooted in my mind, and it will never cease, because of the words of the opponents." It is refuted by what refuted its predecessor. And the noble may be hidden:

Obscurity is no shame
for a man of dignity,
for the Night of Power is hidden,
and that is the best of nights.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 1, verse 1 (part 4 of 6):

I would like to know: was his glorifying of God Most High during his bowing and prostration something blameworthy, so that he hid it, or something good, so that he proclaimed it openly? I do not think ill of the man, for the argument is strong in itself and firmly established in his intellect.

(The Fourth) What al-Shafi'i transmitted from Anas: that Mu'awiya led the people of Medina in prayer and did not recite "In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful" (the basmala). The Muhajirun (Emigrants) and the Ansar (Helpers) objected to him, so he repeated the report in its meaning. His opponents reject this, or it is said: it was not recited in its outward form, and they knew this from some indications. "The one who sees is not like the one who hears."

(The Fifth) What al-Bayhaqi transmitted from Abu Hurayra: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) used to recite the basmala aloud in prayer." This is also related from Umar, his son, Ibn Abbas, and Ibn al-Zubayr. As for Ali, it is said to be widely transmitted from him, and "whoever follows Ali in his religion has been guided." His opponents reject this. And even if it is denied, it may be said that the audible recitation happened at times for a purpose. Moreover, among the reports we have mentioned there is also something that conflicts with attributing it to Umar, Ali, and Ibn Abbas. The claim that it is widely transmitted from Ali is not accepted by the People of the Sunna (Ahl al-Sunna). Yes, the Shi'a claimed it, and so they adopted audible recitation in both silent and audible prayers. Had anyone acted on everything they claim to be widely transmitted from the Commander (Ali), he would have become an unbeliever. So there is nothing but believing in some and disbelieving in others. What he mentioned, that whoever follows Ali in his religion is guided, is accepted. But even if we grant the report of what Ali (may God be pleased with him) did, while setting aside its many difficulties, it is understood that what is common among the People of the Sunna is to prefer what the two Shaykhs (Abu Bakr and Umar) did. And when they differ, then what al-Siddiq (Abu Bakr) did is preferred, since the Prophet (ﷺ) elevated the specification toward him gradually. First he said: "My companions are like stars; whichever of them you follow, you will be guided." Second: "Hold to my sunna and the sunna of the rightly guided Caliphs after me." Third: "Follow the two after me, Abu Bakr and Umar." Fourth: "If you do not find me, then come to Abu Bakr."

(The Sixth) That it is connected to a implied verb, such as: "With the help of the name of God, they set out." There is no doubt that hearing this phrase alerts the intellect that there is no power to refrain from disobeying God except by God's protection, and no strength to obey God except by God's grace. It also alerts it that nothing of the good deeds is complete unless it begins with the mention of God Most High. And to make it apparent is a form of enjoining good. This is rejected, along with the weakness of this estimation and the absence of anyone who holds it. The understanding of the command to good from this sentence requires reflection. If one devoted even a tenth of a tenth of that effort to the verse of God Most High, "You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help," he would obtain many times over, without great harm, and it would suffice in its place. Then he (may God have mercy on him) mentioned words that benefit only in multiplying the blackness of the page and frightening weak students with armies of ink.

(The Third Section on its Meaning) The bāʾ (the letter "bi-") is either for seeking help (li-l-istiʿāna), or for accompaniment (li-l-muṣāḥaba), or for attachment (li-l-ilṣāq), or for elevation (li-l-istiʿlāʾ), or it is extra (zāʾida), or it is an oath (qasamiyya). The last four are nothing, even if some are supported by some verses. There is disagreement about which of the first two is preferred. What al-Baydawi's words suggest is the preference of the first. It is strengthened by the argument that making it for seeking help indicates that the name of God has a greater role in the action, as if the action could not be accomplished or exist without the name of God Most High, and this is not free from subtle grace. What Zamakhshari's words suggest is the preference of the second. It is strengthened by the argument that the bāʾ of accompaniment is more common in usage than the bāʾ of seeking help, especially with meanings and similar verbs. Also, seeking blessing through the name of God Most High is a form of good conduct toward Him and a glorifying of Him, unlike making it an instrument, since instruments are commonplace and not sought for their own sake. Also, the beginning of the polytheists with the names of their gods was for the sake of blessing, so they should be refuted on this point. And if the bāʾ is taken as accompaniment, it is more indicative of the connection of all parts of the action to the name of God Most High than if it is taken as an instrument. This matches what is related in the hadith: "The mention of God Most High is in the heart of every Muslim, whether he mentions it or not." Also, seeking blessing through the name of God Most High is an apparent meaning that everyone who begins with it understands, whereas the interpretation mentioned about its being an instrument is only reached through careful reflection. The name of God Most High being an instrument for the action is only in the sense that it reaches Him through His blessing, so it ultimately returns to the meaning of seeking blessing. So let us say that first. And making the name of God Most High an instrument for reciting the Fatiha is not possible according to the view of one who says that the basmala is part of the surah. And the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "In the name of God, with whose name nothing harms," is something used as supporting evidence for it. In the first case, making the existent perceptible like the non-existent is involved. The name of God is existent in the recitation. So when the bāʾ is taken as seeking help, its course becomes like that of the pen, so it is not recited, but it is recited. Also, in it there is brevity and reaching a greater meaning through fewer words, by estimating: "seeking blessing." And since it is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), it shows the state of the doer. It has been established that every action performed for the sake of drawing near to God Most High requires His help, may His majesty be exalted, so the circumstance indicates an additional meaning. In my view, seeking help is preferable, and it is nearly required. For in it there is more courtesy, humility, and showing servitude than there is in the claim of accompaniment. Also, it contains an allusion from the first moment to the removal of power and strength, and the negation of the independent capacity of servants and its effect. It is an opening of the door of mercy and a winning of a treasure: "There is no power and no strength except in God." Also, this meaning is more closely connected to the verse "and You alone we ask for help." Also, it is almost required in the verse "Recite in the name of your Lord," so that it may be an answer to the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying "I am not a reciter," in the most complete and perfect way. And everything they mentioned in support of accompaniment is rejected. (As for the first) it is because, without establishing the majority, it is like trying to pluck thorns (an impossible task). (As for the second) it is because it is a delusion arising from their illustrating the instrument with perceptible things. Not every seeking of help is through a degraded instrument. There is no doubt about the correctness of "I sought help from God," and it has come in the Law: "Seek help in God and be steadfast." So the aspect of degradation does not even come to mind, and the heart is surrounded by another aspect. Also, there is a consideration in restricting seeking help to the instrument, for it may be through it, and through power. And even if it is granted, what prevents indicating here that, just as He is the one intended in essence, He is also the one intended indirectly, since there is no power or strength except by Him?

(As for the third) it is because the polytheists are closer to seeking help through their gods, since they are their intermediaries in drawing near to God Most High, and these are more like an instrument.

(As for the fourth) it is because an instrument must exist in every part until the end of the action, otherwise the action would not be completed. We do not grant the necessity between a thing's accompanying another and its connection to all its parts. As for what he mentioned from the hadith, it is more suitable for seeking help, because it indicates the servant's disavowal of his own power and strength, and the affirmation of power and strength to God Most High. This is among the creedal matters upon which the heart of every Muslim is set, whether he mentions the name or not.

(As for the fifth) it is because if he means that the meaning of accompaniment is blessing, this is clearly invalid, and he returned empty-handed. And if he means that it is understood from it by means of an indicator, then we claim this as well, when the intention is the instrumental sense, because the legal validity of the act depends on it. As for seeking blessing being an apparent meaning for everyone, we do not grant that it is specific to accompaniment.

(As for the sixth) it is because restricting it to that is disputed. As for the seventh, there is no barrier to what something begins with being a part of it. The Fatiha is the opening of the Qur'an and part of it. And even if it is granted that it is an opening only in relation to what is other than it, as al-Shihab said, the Hanafi is not harmed by what it contains.

(As for the eighth) it is because the meaning of the hadith is: "I do such and such, seeking help with the name of God, with whose name, mentioned while seeking help through it, nothing harms me." For whoever seeks help through His presence, He helps him, and whoever takes refuge at His door, He protects him and preserves him. And even if this is considered far-fetched, and I reject what was said in refutation, namely that what is meant by the hadith is the information that nothing of creation harms one who mentions His name, and that accompaniment requires something already present with it, like: "The Messenger has come to you with the truth," while the recitation has not yet taken place, so the literal sense of accompaniment is impossible. Yet the accompaniment here is not perceptible. And that it is an information about the negation of the companionship of harm is understood from it as the companionship of benefit and blessing, which is the repelling of whispering from the reciter together with abundant reward. So there is no harm in this either, for it is merely a source of comfort, and it does not unsettle us, since what we find comfort in is plentiful.

(As for the ninth) it is because making the existent like the non-existent for the sake of the flow of the rhetorical embellishment is not in accordance with what is required. The point here is that the name of God is likened, on the basis of the believer's certainty about what has come in the Sunna and his conviction of its requirement, to a perceptible matter: the appearance of writings by the pen, and their non-appearance when it is absent. Then it was expressed as an implied metaphor (isti'āra tabʿiyya) because it occurs in the particle.

(As for the tenth) it is because the state of the comparison with the pen is not hidden.

(As for the eleventh) it is because we do not grant that blessing is the meaning of accompaniment or a necessary part of its meaning. Rather, it is known from an external matter, which is that the accompaniment of His name, glorified is He, is accompanied by that. This also applies to seeking help through His name, mighty is His majesty, and in seeking help there is a grace that is not hidden. It is possible, though a stretch, that Zamakhshari's not choosing it was due to the Mu'tazili whisperings of the Devil, namely the independence of the servant in his action. For he and his companions held this view, and God willing, its refutation will come later. There has been disagreement about the object of the preposition. Imam Ibn Jarir took the view of estimating it as: "I recite," because the reciter of something is recited. In this way, a specific verbal action is implied for every doer of an action, making the naming a beginning for it. This is among the Qur'anic meanings, like its counterparts, because they are necessary in common language usage. By this, the statement of al-Sadiqi is refuted. The intended one here is not a specific speaker, so it is of one kind. Even if one says "Recite," each one intends himself with the pronoun. So its precedence over the recitation of this reciter does no harm, nor over its existence. And it can be easily said that it is a part of the whole or of the part. Since this was obscure to some, they made the estimated verb an imperative directed at the servants, so that the speaker of the spoken and the estimated would be unified. Al-Farra' chose this deliberately, and it is related from Ibn Abbas, because God Most High placed the naming first, urging the servants to do so. This is what suits instruction. The grammarians went to estimating it generally, as in: "I begin." This was supported by several arguments. Among them: the verb of beginning can be estimated in every naming, unlike the verb of recitation. And estimating the general is preferable. Do you not see that they estimate the object of the preposition when it is a predicate, an attribute, a circumstantial clause, or a relative clause, as "being" and "being established," wherever it occurs, and they prefer it because of its general validity of estimation?

(Among them) that it independently serves the purpose of the naming, which is its occurrence as an inceptive beginning. So estimating it fits the place better. When you estimate "I recite," you are estimating "I begin with the recitation," because what occurs in the middle of it is also a recitation, and the basmala is not legislated in it. Among them is the manifestation of the verb of beginning in the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Every important matter which is not begun with the name of God is cut off." As for the manifestation of the recitation in the verse "Recite in the name of your Lord," it is because the more important there is the recitation itself, and it is not viewed in relation to its beginning. That is why the verb was placed first. This is not the case with the naming.

What is attributed to the Imam is closer to the purpose, more specific to the intended meaning, and more comprehensive in scope. It implies that the recitation takes place in its entirety, joined with the basmala, seeking help through the Name of God Most High in all of it. This contrasts with the estimate "I begin" (أبتدئ), since there is no indication of that. As for what was mentioned first, namely citing the grammarians' estimate of "existing" and "being established" (الكون والاستقرار), it is not sound, because they did this as an illustration, where they do not intend a specific governing word but rather speak of the governing word in general. It is like their illustration with Zayd and 'Amr, not for their particular identities, but so that the discussion falls on an example, which is closer to understanding. It cannot be said that if the agent is left unspecified, it is estimated as one of these two, on the grounds that "beginning" (الابتداء) here is not more general than the recitation, because what is meant by it is the beginning of the recitation, which is more specific than the recitation, since it applies to the recitation of the first part, the middle, and the last, while the beginning of the recitation is specific to the first part. So this is not the existing and being established that the grammarians estimated earlier. The claim that "I begin" (أبتدئ) is general, on the basis that it is treated as intransitive, but it is known from the context that the thing begun is the recitation, or on the basis of the original governing word in all cases, is clearly flawed. When the context indicates its intended meaning, what is the sense of treating it as intransitive then? Its being based on the wording and the original form does not remove the objection in any case. So understand this. As for what was mentioned second, namely that the response to the act of beginning is independently sufficient for the purpose, this is not granted. We have already stated that the recitation is more specific and more comprehensive, and that the occurrence of the beginning is by the act of beginning itself, not by an implied beginning. Whoever begins with the basmala attains the purpose without needing anything else, just as one who prays and begins with the takbir of opening does not need an implied element to be a beginner, but he does need its blessing and its comprehensiveness for everything he does. From this it becomes clear what weakness is in the rest of the discussion. (As for what was mentioned third), it is that the basmala being the thing begun with is achieved in actuality, not by an implied verb. The hadith does not say: "Every matter of importance in which one does not say or imply 'in the name of God' is incomplete." Furthermore, the preservation of agreement with the wording of the hadith is fitting only as a point of refinement in the speech of the authors and those who follow their path, not in the speech of God, majestic is His glory, as is not hidden from anyone with a sound disposition. Also, the investigation concerns preferring the estimate of a general verb, such as "I begin" or "I commence" and what resembles them, not preferring the particular "I recite," meaning a verb whose verbal noun is recitation, over the particular "I begin," meaning a verb whose verbal noun is beginning. Therefore, what was mentioned involves departing from the rules of good conduct and the point of dispute.

Some have chosen to estimate "my beginning" (ابتدائي), for example. In this there is an additional implied element, since the predicate must then be implied, so the implied element becomes three words. The indication of nominality for permanence conflicts with the indication of the present tense for continuous renewal, which suits the context, except that the difference between the sentence of the basmala and the sentence of praise (الحمد) remains. Perhaps the matter here is easy. The Greatest Shaykh, may God sanctify his secret, made this prepositional phrase the predicate of an implied subject, which is the beginning of the world and its manifestation, because the cause of its existence is the Divine Names, and they are the ones exercising authority over it. This is like making it dependent on what follows, since God Most High is not praised except through His Names, by way of allusion. So one does not look at the outward meaning in this, nor is it bound by the rules. I do not see objecting to it as fair. Many have held that estimating the dependent element here as delayed is more appropriate, because the Name of God Most High precedes the verb in essence, so it should precede the verb in mention. In this there is an allusion to the demonstration from cause (البرهان اللمي), which is more noble than the demonstration from effect (البرهان الأني). For this reason one of the knowers said: "I have not seen anything without seeing God before it." Soothing the child of the intellect with the sweetness of this Name helps wean it from sucking the udder of the ordinary, without the bitterness of createdness being imposed. Moreover, the blessing of seeking blessing overflows with importance. And if we say that in the preceding there is a cutting of the root of the thorn, a refutation of those who claim it, this suits the station of prophethood. The secret of placing the verb first in the first verse revealed is also clear, since the station at that time was a station of prophethood, with no refutation and no conveying in it. Every station has its own speech. Eloquence is the conformity of speech to what the situation requires. The understandings have struggled here in explaining the restriction (القصر), since it is supposed from the mention of exclusivity, to the extent that some claimed it in all three of its types, and some singled out a type, so one limits it to restriction of singularity (قصر الإفراد) and holds it, along with inversion (القلب), and within inversion there is every kind. In my view, here it is estimated as preceding. Most scholars also hold this. The estimate of it as delayed is removed from the courtyard of verification, because it would be either estimated after the preposition "bi" (با), or after a noun, or after the Name of God, or after the end of the sentence. As for estimating it after the preposition "bi," no one who knows the preposition would say it. As for after the noun, it entails separation, even if mentally, since they required the omission here between the two elements of a genitive construction (المتضايفين). As for after the Name of God, it entails separation in the same way between the attribute and the described. As for between the two attributes, the breach widens. As for after the completion of the sentence, a subtle deficiency appears, because in the sentence the ruling is tied to something that suggests causation. So "the Most Merciful, the Compassionate" becomes a cause for the recitation restricted to the Name of God. When the restricted governing element is delayed, and its cause is placed first, it suggests limitation, and its aspect is not clear. When we estimate the governing element as preceding, as is the original, we are safe from the prohibited, and exclusivity is achieved as well, since it is as if it were said, for example: "I recite seeking help or seeking blessing through the Name of God, the Most Merciful, the Compassionate, because He is the Most Merciful, the Compassionate." When the cause is absent, the effect is absent in the rhetorical context, if no other cause appears, so this yields exclusivity, especially according to the one who holds the principle of the attribute's implication (مفهوم الصفة). So it suggests that whoever is not characterized by that is outside the circle. The restriction here is not like the restriction there. The escape by estimating the construction "seeking help through the Name of God, because He is the Most Merciful, the Compassionate, I recite" contains what is not hidden from a sound disposition. In placing the createdness first in the mind and omitting it in mention, and in the absence of anything manifest standing independently apart from the eternal Name, there is a hidden symbol pointing to the precedence of the fixed entities in knowledge, even if that is not upon the existence of God Most High, since to Him, majestic is His glory, belongs absolute precedence, and the non-appearance of anything other than Him. "Everything perishes except His Face." And to indicate that there is no harm in this, it is undertaken. Seeking blessing, like obligation, requires precedence in mention with a kasra, not a damma. Here it is, as you see. Among the great ones someone said: "I have not seen anything without seeing God Most High in it," and there is no indwelling. This has been counted more perfect than the first, and the stations are four. Soothing with mercy suffices instead of every milk, and weans the child of the intellect from the breast of the maidens of thought. It is as if whoever estimated the governing element as delayed saw "In the name of God is its course" (Qur'an 11:41), and "In Your name, my Lord, I lay down my side," and similar examples, so it followed their course. The difference is clear to the observer. This is one of the breezes of the dawn, so awaken to it and sleep to other than it.

The adverbial phrase (الظرف) is "stable" (مستقر) according to some, and "trivial" (لغو) according to others. Their interpretations have differed. It was said: the trivial is that whose governing element is mentioned, and the stable is that whose governing element is entirely omitted. It was also said: the stable is that whose governing element is general, such as "existence" (الحصول) and "establishment" (الاستقرار), and it is estimated, while the trivial is the opposite. It was said: the trivial is that whose governing element is outside the adverbial phrase and not understood from it, whether it is mentioned or not, while the stable is that from which the meaning of its estimated governing element is understood, which is one of the general verbs. All of this is terminology, and where there is no dispute about it, I choose the first. So the adverbial phrase here is stable, however the governing element is estimated. The letter "bi" (باء) was given a kasra, although the rule for single particles is that they be given a fatha, because they are built (مبنية), and the basis for building is its heaviness. Its being opposite to the existential case-ending is a damma for its lightness, and its being non-existential... However, from the standpoint that they are words in themselves, they are liable to begin, and beginning with a quiescent letter is impossible or difficult, so their proper vowel was the fatha, since it is the brother of quiescence in the desired lightness in what turns frequently on the tongues, distinguished among the letters by necessarily being particles and by governing the genitive. Each of these suits the kasra. As for being a particle, it requires absence of movement, and the kasra, since it is scarce, does not occur in the verb, nor in the indeclinable noun, nor in particles except rarely, and suits absence. As for the genitive, the vowel of "bi" agrees with its effect. There is no counterexample from the conjunction "wa" (واو العطف), which is necessarily a particle, nor from the comparative "ka" (كاف التشبيه), which necessarily governs the genitive, because the combination is the cause of distinction, and it is not found in each one separately. But the counterexample remains in the oath "wa" (واو القسم) and its "ta" (تاء القسم). It is answered that its governing is by deputy for "bi," which is the original of its letters, so the genitive is as if it were not an effect of these two. These are grammatical reasons derived after the fact to show suitability, so they do not bear critique because of their weakness, as it was said:

"The covenant of the one I love and his pact
are weaker than the argument of a grammarian."

So we shall not keep the eyelid of thought awake over what is for it and against it. Some said, from the standpoint of allusion: the "bi" in the basmala was given a kasra to teach the way of reaching God Most High and attaching oneself to His Names through lowering the side, submission, and the humility of servanthood. One does not reach any kind of knowledge except through some kind of humiliation and breaking. As the Shaykh Umar ibn al-Farid, may God sanctify his overflowing secret, indicated in his saying:

"If you were, for me, a lowering from the dot of the 'ba',
you would be raised to what you have not attained by stratagem.

To the point that you see that you do not see what you have counted,
and that what you have prepared is not a preparation."

Lowering is the opposite of raising. Whoever is lowered by the consideration of the humiliation of servanthood is raised by destiny to the contemplation of the might of lordship. This raising is not attained by stratagem, but is purely a sublime divine gift. Whoever descends in order to rise, his descent is causally conditioned, and his striving is not accepted. End of quotation.

This is a matter specific to the "ba" of the basmala, and it cannot apply to the "ba" of genitive in general, as is not hidden. In my view, the secret of this is that the "ba" is the second level in relation to the simple, unadorned alif, which precedes all the levels. So it is an allusion to the true existence. The "ba" is either an allusion to His attributes, which the dot of existence has made manifest. For this reason, when it was said to the knower al-Shibli, "Are you al-Shibli?" he said, "I am the dot beneath the 'ba'." The Greatest Shaykh, may God sanctify his secret, said:

"The 'ba' for the knower al-Shibli is considered,
and in its dot there is a reminder for the heart.
The secret of the exalted servanthood has mixed with it,
therefore it took the place of the Truth, so take heed.

Is not the name is dropped from 'bismi' its reality,
because it is a substitute for it? This is a burden."

The attributes are either of beauty (jamaliyya) or of majesty (jalaliyya). The attributes of beauty take precedence, as the hadith indicates: "My mercy has preceded My wrath." The letter *bāʾ* (in *bismi*) is a sign of them, because it is the intermediary in bestowal and outpouring. Thus the kasra and the lowering of the wing (the *bāʾ* is written with a kasra) are appropriate, so that the matter may be completed and the secret may appear. Beginning with it here hastens the glad tidings, and it is a symbol that the axis of everything is mercy, as the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "None of you will enter Paradise by his deeds alone." They asked: "Not even you, Messenger of Allah?" He said: "Not even I, unless Allah covers me with His mercy." Glory be to Him, He progressed in revealing it: He alluded to it with the *bāʾ*, pointed to it with "Allah", and stated it most clearly with "the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate."

As for an allusion to the Muhammadan Reality (al-ḥaqīqa al-Muḥammadiyya, the spiritual reality of the Prophet (ﷺ)) and the first determination (al-taʿayyun al-awwal) referred to in his (ﷺ) saying, "The first thing Allah created was the light of your Prophet, O Jabir," and through which the outpouring took place, as is indicated by "Had it not been for you, I would not have created the spheres": and because mercy predominates in him (ﷺ), especially towards the believers of his community, as indicated by the words of Allah, the Exalted: "We have sent you only as a mercy to the worlds" and His words: "to the believers, kind and merciful" (9:128). This fits the appearance of the kasra in what points to his rank. Beginning with it here is also a symbol of the attribute of the one to whom the Book was revealed and of the one who calls to Allah. Together with the statement of the attribute of the One being called to, that He is the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate, this creates complete eagerness and great encouragement.

Glory be to Him, He also progressed in describing His Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) with this in the Qur'an, until He said: "And indeed you are of a great character" (68:4). He was content with the symbol here because the effects had not yet appeared, and "the first of the rain is a drop, then it pours down." No surah is opened except that the Lord opened it with a symbol of the state of the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace), honouring him, and as glad tidings to whoever gives ear while he is a witness. Since majesty is evident in Surah Bara'a (al-Tawba), He omitted the basmala there and used an open *bāʾ* (in a different form) because the state had changed, and to draw the veil over the brides of beauty. Glory be to Him, He did not entirely abandon the symbol of the Muhammadan Reality. We cannot express more than this on this subject, for fear of the reproach of the people of the veil, and behind it lies a great secret. Allah, the Exalted, is the Guide to the straight path.

The *ism* (name), according to the Basrans, is one of the ten nouns whose initial letters are built on sukun. They are: *ibn* (son), *ibnat* (daughter), *ibnum*, *ism* (name), *ist*, *ithnān* (two, masc.), *ithnatān* (two, fem.), *imruʾ* (man), *imraʾa* (woman), *aymunu-llāh* (by Allah's right) and *aymu-llāh minhu*. Otherwise they are eleven, if *ibnim* is counted. When they are pronounced, they add a hamza, because starting with a consonant that is not a long vowel (al-madd) is disliked among them, and in these it is impossible. The matter is one of taste. It is among the words whose final part has been deleted, like *yad* (hand). Of those mentioned, all except the last three.

Its origin is *sumuww* (height). The *wāw* was deleted for lightness, due to frequent use and the alternation of vowels. The *sīn* was made quiescent and the *mīm* was vowelled. The hamzat al-waṣl (the connecting hamza) was added, so its pattern is *ifʿ*. Its inflections include *asmāʾ* (names) and *sumayy* and *summiyat*, unlike *awsām*, *wasīm* and *wasamtu* (I marked), which bears witness to it. A wound on the heart is not accepted. Its derivation is from *sumuww*, like *ʿuluww* (height), because by indicating its referent it raises it from the depths of obscurity to the peak of manifestation and clarity.

The Kufans said: it is from *simah* (mark), because it is a sign of its referent, and its origin is *wasm*. The *wāw* was deleted and the hamzat al-waṣl was substituted for it. Its pattern is *iʿl*. This is refuted by the fact that a hamza is not known to be attached to something whose initial part has been deleted. Adding an alteration (iʿlāl) is more analogous than the absence of a parallel. Also, that it is a substitute requires that it be intended for its own sake, while being a connector requires that it be intended secondarily; a substitute is like a part of the root and not like a connector. Thus it is a combination of two things. Therefore it was said: there is neither deletion nor substitution; rather the *wāw* was changed into a hamza, as in *iʿāʾ* and *ishāḥ*. Then its use became frequent, so its hamza was made a connecting hamza. It may be pronounced as a cut hamza for necessity. The first view is preferred because of that testimony.

It has dialects which some have brought up to eighteen, and one has versified them, saying:

"The *ism* has ten dialects along with eight, / according to the transmission of my grandfather, the shaykh of the people, the most complete of them.
*Sm*, *simāt*, *sama*, *ism*; add *sima*, / likewise *samāʾ*, with three vowels for its first letter."

Furthermore, the dispute has long been prolonged over whether the *ism* is identical with the named (al-musammā) or other than it. The Ash'aris hold the first, and the Mu'tazilites hold the second. The eminent scholars have been perplexed in determining the place of the discussion in a way that would be worthy of this dispute. So much so that our master al-Fakhr said in al-Tafsir al-Kabir: this discussion is like folly. He mentioned a point which he claimed was subtle and precise. Al-Shihab has spared us the burden of refuting it. The distinguished master (al-Sayyid) wished in Sharh al-Mawaqif to do so, but it was not completed for him. Al-Suhayli had a statement on the subject which he claimed was the truth. Ibn al-Sayyid wrote a separate treatise refuting it. Al-Shihab claimed that up to now it has not been properly settled, and that he had not seen, despite his wide knowledge of this question, anything that brings satisfaction to the hearts or cures the thirst. May Allah have mercy on him: in his glosses on al-Baydawi he did not come up, from his own opinion, with anything that removes the difficulty and relieves the mind. Here I am, by the grace of Allah, mentioning something which, if accepted, is the utmost of what I hope for. Sometimes what is found in the omission is not found in the omission itself. And if it is refuted, then the words of thousands were refuted before me, each one of whom is a single individual confronting rows of troops.

"When the young camel (ibn al-labūn) is tied up in a rope, / it cannot withstand the attack of the stallion camels."

**Surat al-Fatiha (The Opening Chapter of the Book)**

Scholars have differed about this surah. Most hold that it is Meccan, and some say it was among the first parts of the Qur'an to be revealed. This is the view narrated from Ali, Ibn Abbas, Qatadah, and most of the Companions. Mujahid alone held that it is Medinan, and this view is regarded as an unusual lapse on his part. It has also been said that it was revealed in Mecca when the prayer was prescribed and in Medina when the *qiblah* (direction of prayer) was changed, so that it would be known that it belongs to the prayer as it was.
