Then, Exalted is He, removed seven letters from this surah, which are the initial words indicating punishment, as a reminder that whoever recites this surah, believes in it, and knows its realities, becomes safe from the seven levels of Hell." End of quote. What is in it is not hidden, and his answer neither benefits him nor suffices him. For someone may say: then let the *dhāl*, *wāw*, *nūn*, *ḥā'*, *ʿayn*, *mīm*, and *ghayn* be omitted as well, since the *wāw* is from *wayl* (woe), the *dhāl* from *dhilla* (humiliation), the *nūn* from *nār* (fire), the *ḥā'* from *ḥamīm* (boiling water), the *ʿayn* from *ʿadhāb* (punishment), the *mīm* from *mihād* (bed/resting place), and the *ghayn* from *ghawāshī* (overwhelming things). The verses are evident, and all of them concern the people of the Fire. The benefit of omitting these would be like the benefit of omitting those, without any difference at all. Moreover, in his words, may God Exalted have mercy on him, there is something other than this. Indeed, even granting that his statement is free from what has been said or may be said, I do not approve of it for Fakhr, who is the master who became the felicity of the religion, the proof of Islam, and the defender of its people.

As for attributing it to the Commander of the Faithful, ʿAlī, may God honour his face, when Caesar of Rome asked Muʿāwiya about this and he did not answer, so he asked ʿAlī and he answered: there is no basis for it. And even on the assumption of its acceptance, what was the Commander's purpose in being content with this measure, except to alert the questioner to secrets that are not hidden from you? So understand this, and may God Exalted take care of your guidance.

(Fifth, sixth, and seventh names): *al-Kanz* (the Treasure), *al-Wāfiyah* (the Sufficient), and *al-Kāfiyah* (the Adequate), because of what has been mentioned about its inclusion of hidden jewels; it suffices and is sufficient. Or because it is not halved in prayer, and nothing else can substitute for it in prayer.

(Eighth): *al-Asās* (the Foundation), because it is the origin of the Qur'an and the first surah in it.

(Ninth, tenth, eleventh, twelfth, and thirteenth): the Surah of Praise, the Surah of Gratitude, the Surah of Supplication, the Surah of Teaching the Request, and the Surah of Asking, because of its inclusion of these. As for its inclusion of praise, it is evident. Likewise gratitude, for whoever has been blessed by God with understanding. It is possible that these names are like "the Mother of the Qur'an" and "the Mother of the Book."

As for its inclusion of the third (ethics), it is like its inclusion of the first, rather more evident. As for teaching the request, it is because it begins with praise before it. The fifth is like the third, and these two are like those two, the third and fourth, as is not hidden.

(Fourteenth and fifteenth): the Surah of Intimate Conversation (*al-munājāh*) and the Surah of Delegation (*al-tafwīd*), because the servant converses with his Lord by saying: ﴿You alone we worship and You alone we ask for help﴾, and by this, delegation is achieved.

(Sixteenth, seventeenth, and eighteenth): the Incantation (*al-ruqyah*), the Cure (*al-shifā'*), and the Healing (*al-shāfiyah*). The authentic hadiths indicate this.

(Nineteenth): the Surah of Prayer, because it is obligatory or a pillar (*farīḍah*) in it. Recommendation is the view of some jurists, and a narration from some regarding voluntary prayer. It has been said: among its names is "the Prayer," based on the hadith: "I have divided the prayer between Me and My servant into two halves." He meant the surah. The linguistic metonymy, by the relation of the whole and the part, or of necessity, actually or by ruling, like the metonymy in ellipsis, is possible.

(Twentieth): *al-Nūr* (the Light), either because it is apparent through its frequent use, or because it illuminates hearts due to the greatness of its rank, or because what it contains of meanings is an expression of the light, meaning the Qur'an.

(Twenty-first): *al-Qur'ān al-ʿAẓīm* (the Great Qur'an), which is evident from what we have previously presented.

(Twenty-second): *al-Sabʿ al-Mathānī* (the Seven Oft-Repeated), because it consists of seven verses by consensus, and we have not seen anything sharing this except "Ara'ayta" (Surah al-Ma'un). The claim that it has eight verses is like the claim that it has nine; it is an anomalous view that does not deserve attention, or it is an error by a narrator. However, some counted the basmala as a verse but not "those upon whom You have bestowed favour," and some did the reverse, and the basis is the transmission. The second opinion is not weakened by the fact that the length of this verse does not correspond to the length of the verse-endings of other surahs. Moreover, in Surah al-Nasr there is something of this kind. It is repeated (*tuthannā*) and repeated (*tukarrar*) in every rak'ah and in every prayer containing bowing. Or the intended meaning is the common and usual meaning of prayer, so a single rak'ah is not objected to, nor is the funeral prayer. Moreover, there is disagreement concerning the *batīrā'* (a prayer without tashahhud), and the funeral prayer is a supplication, not a prayer in the true sense. It has been said that it is described by this because it is repeated (*tuthannā*) with another surah, or because it was revealed twice, or because it is of two kinds: supplication and praise, or because whenever the servant recites one verse of it, God repeats it by reporting His action, as in the well-known hadith. Other statements have also been made. These statements are based on the assumption that *mathānī* comes from *tathniyah* (repetition). It is possible that it comes from *thanā'* (praise), because it contains praise of God, or because of what is reported of praise for whoever recites it. It is also possible that it comes from *thunyā* (exception), because God has singled it out for this Community, and to God belongs praise for this blessing.

Then, the wisdom in the Qur'an being divided into surahs, like books, contrary to al-Zarkashi's view, is that it is more energizing for the reciter and more motivating for acquiring knowledge, like the traveller who, when he covers a mile or a league, refreshes himself by it and becomes energetic for the journey. When the memorizer takes a surah, he believes he has taken from the Book of God a distinct portion, and so what he has memorized becomes great in his eyes. Also, when a genus includes various types and kinds, it is better than if it had only one chapter beneath it. Along with this, there is in it a confirmation that the surah by itself is a miracle and one of the signs of God, Exalted is He. The wisdom in its being long and short is more evident than to be hidden.

**Surat al-Fatiha (The Opening Chapter of the Book)**

Scholars have differed about this surah. Most hold that it is Meccan, and some say it was among the first parts of the Qur'an to be revealed. This is the view narrated from Ali, Ibn Abbas, Qatadah, and most of the Companions. Mujahid alone held that it is Medinan, and this view is regarded as an unusual lapse on his part. It has also been said that it was revealed in Mecca when the prayer was prescribed and in Medina when the *qiblah* (direction of prayer) was changed, so that it would be known that it belongs to the prayer as it was. It has also been said that part of it is Meccan and part Medinan, but the weakness of this view is clear. People have commonly argued for its Meccan origin from the verse of al-Hijr: ﴿And We have certainly given you seven of the oft-repeated [verses] and the Great Qur'an﴾. This is a Meccan surah according to the explicit statement of the scholars and a report from Ibn Abbas. It has the status of a *marfu'* report (one traced back to the Prophet), not because what precedes and follows it concerns the people of Mecca, as has been said, because that rests on the premise that a Meccan revelation is one addressed to the people of Mecca, whereas the well-known view is otherwise. The stronger argument is the transmission from the Companions who witnessed the revelation and descent of the Qur'an, for this rests first on interpreting "the seven oft-repeated" as referring to al-Fatiha. Although this is sound and established in the hadiths, it is also soundly reported from Ibn Abbas and others that it refers to the seven long surahs. Second, the argument rests on the impossibility of bestowing a favour through something before it is given, whereas God Most High has bestowed favours upon Him (ﷺ) before giving them, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, We have granted you a clear victory﴾. This was revealed years before the conquest, and the use of the past tense indicates the certainty of its occurrence. Although this is contrary to the apparent meaning, especially with the presence of the particle *lam* and the word *qad*, and its occurrence in the context of a favour (where the usual sense is that the event has already taken place), and the sequence ﴿And do not strain your eyes toward what We have given to some pairs of them﴾, the argument has nevertheless been challenged. It cannot be said that this and that only indicate that the surah was revealed in Mecca, and not that it was not revealed in Medina, because we reply: negation is the default, and the one who claims affirmation must establish it, and how can he do so? As for what they said in answer to the objection, that descent is the appearance from the unseen world into the visible one, and that appearance in the visible world does not admit of repetition, for the appearance of something apparent is itself manifestly void, like obtaining what is already obtained, based on the claim that it was revealed in each case for a purpose, or that it was revealed in one manner once and another manner another time because of the occurrence of the variant readings *Malik* and *Malik*, or with *Basmalah* at times and without it at others, and the gathering of these views and reports only confirms the occurrence (of revelation in both places) without necessitating it, as is clear.

The surah is written with a hamza and without a hamza, with substitution, if it derives from *su'r*, which means remainder, because the remainder of everything is a part of it. Without the hamza, if it derives from *sur al-bina'* (the wall of a building), which means a station, or *sur al-madinah* (the wall of a city), because it encloses its verses, or from *tasawwur*, which means height and elevation, because it is elevated by being the speech of God Most High. It is also used for a lofty station, as in the words of al-Nabigha:

*Have you not seen that God has given you a surah?*
*You see every angel around it swaying.*

The Qur'an has unified it as one comprising a beginning and an end. It has also been said that it is a distinct section, so that the verse of the Throne (*Ayat al-Kursi*) is excluded, being a distinct verse by tradition. The names of all the surahs are established by hadiths and reports. Whoever holds that it is disliked to say "the surah of such-and-such," but rather "a surah in which such-and-such is mentioned," on the basis of what is reported from Anas and Ibn Umar prohibiting this, is not to be relied upon, since the hadith from Anas is weak or fabricated, and the hadith from Ibn Umar is a statement of his own (*mawquf*), even if it is reported from him with a sound chain.

*Al-Fatihah* is in origin an adjective, given either as the name for the first part of a thing because it is the means of opening the whole, with the *ta'* marking transmission (from adjective to noun) or intensification. It is not restricted to the pattern of a sign or to a verbal noun. It was applied to the first thing by designating the object by the verbal noun, to indicate its primacy, as if it were the very act of opening, since its connection to the opening is first, and then through it the whole collection is connected, being a part of it. The same is said of *al-Khatimah* (the conclusion), for reaching the end first befalls the last part, and the whole is through it. This is not like the first case, because the form *fa'ilah* is rare among verbal nouns. Nevertheless, it is preferable to say that it is not an instrument or a motive, because these are linked to the act and accompany it, and it is generally the case that an instrument does not have the attribute and a motive does not accompany the act. Moreover, the instrumental sense is unsuitable here, since it would imply that some part is not intended. They also permitted it to be an attributive relation, meaning "possessing an opening," along with other less preferred possibilities.

"The Book" is the individual collected whole. The opening of al-Fatihah is in relation to this whole, not to the common concept shared between it and its parts. This is realised in the knowledge, or the Tablet, or the House of Honour (*Bayt al-'Izzah*). There is no harm in the surah being known by this name from early times. The first idiom is the annexation of a name to what it names, which is well known. The second idiom means *li*, the sense of belonging, as in "a part of a thing," not *min* (of), as in "a ring of silver," because the annexed term is partial. This was said by Shaykh al-Islam, and it is the view of some concerning all such cases. Ibn Kaysan and al-Sirafi said that the annexation of a part is in the sense of the partitive *min*. In the *Lumma'* and its commentary it is said that *min* implied in annexation is in general of this kind, without distinguishing between a part and a partial term. Some made the annexation of a partial term explanatory in all cases, and some restricted it to a relation of general and specific overlap, as in the example, and made it a *lam* relation in the absolute case, like "the city of Baghdad." The common usage does not support this.

This noble surah has names which some have counted at over twenty. One of them is *Fatihat al-Kitab* (The Opening of the Book), because it is the beginning of the Book in its known order, not because it is recited at the beginning of teaching or the recitation in prayer, as the Imam al-Suyuti supposed, nor because it was the first surah revealed, as has been said. As for the first and third names, the priority in terms of teaching or revelation requires observing the order in the rest of the parts of the Book from those two aspects. There is no doubt that the order of teaching and the order of revelation are not like the known order. As for the second name, you know that the meaning of "the Book" is not the common concept applying to what is recited in prayer, so that its priority to it would be considered in the naming. Al-Mursi related that it was called this because it is the first surah written on the Tablet. This needs transmission. Even if we affirm that the order of the Qur'an in our codices is as in the Tablet, it may be that the follower was written and then the one followed was written. Strong probability is a separate matter.

The second name is *Fatihat al-Qur'an* (The Opening of the Qur'an), for the reason we have already mentioned, exactly in the same manner.

The third and fourth names are *Umm al-Kitab* (The Mother of the Book) and *Umm al-Qur'an* (The Mother of the Qur'an). The hadith "Let none of you say *Umm al-Kitab*; let him say *Fatihat al-Kitab*" has no basis. Indeed, its being named this is established in the sound collections, as will not be hidden from one who examines them. It was named this because the beginning, whether in writing, recitation, or descent according to one view, or in prayer with it, and what follows it is a follower of it. So it is like the mother upon whom the child is formed afterwards. The word *umm* is also used for a standard, because it precedes and the army follows it, and from this comes *Umm al-Qura* (the Mother of Cities). Or because it comprises, as the scholar (*al-'Allamah*) said, the principal meanings in the Qur'an: praise of God Most High with what He is worthy of, worship through command and prohibition, and warning. As for praise, it is obvious. As for worship, it arises either from ﴿Praise be to God﴾, because it is for teaching, so a command is implied which it conveys, and the affirmative command necessarily entails a generic prohibition of its opposite, which we do not regard as objectionable. Or from ﴿Guide us to the straight path﴾, if by it is meant the religion of Islam. Or from the supposition "Say: In the name of God," with its complement delayed. As for worship from ﴿You alone we worship﴾, it is an announcement of its exclusive devotion to worship, which is the realisation of servanthood by carrying out what the Master commands or forbids. This indicates in general that they are obliged to worship. It is not objected against the Mu'tazilah (a rationalist theological school) that there was no prior command or prohibition at all. We answer, once the absence of prior command is granted, that the foundation of worship is monotheism, and the opening suggests this. Especially since the Prophet (ﷺ) was already charged with monotheism and conveying the surah, and this suffices. As for promise and warning, they come from God Most High's words ﴿the way of those upon whom You have bestowed favour, not of those who have incurred wrath﴾, or from ﴿the Day of Judgement﴾, meaning the recompense. What is recompensed is either what gladdens or what harms, namely reward and punishment. These purposes apply because the sending of messengers and the revelation of books are a mercy to the servants and guidance towards what sets their lives and their final returns right. This is achieved by knowing who is able to bring blessings into being, and sustain them, and then by reaching Him through what binds what is present, draws more, and in practice and belief, and by freeing oneself from what leads to losing what has been gained and prevents what has been obtained, in heart and body. Praise is the branch of knowing the one praised together with his deserving it. This includes knowledge of the attributes of majesty and beauty, among which are those by which messengers are sent and books revealed, and the difference between the obedient and the sinner. Thus belief in God Most High, His attributes, the prophethood, and the Return enters in general. Worship is made possible by these, and in it enters, by way of belief, the prophethood and what relates to it, including the Book and the angels, since command and prohibition are a branch of the established truth of these in general. Promise and warning imply belief in the Return and stir one to worship. People are like a hundred camels, among which you find no riding camel. Most are moved by desire and fear, the middling ones by hope and dread, and the elect, though few, by intimacy and awe. By these three the guidance to the interests of this life and the next is complete. I do not confine for you the way of restriction to this, for the path of the mind has room. You may reduce the three to two, by including praise within worship, since the mind has no judgement. Perhaps he (al-Zamakhshari) made it a separate division from it as a hint that gratitude to the Benefactor is obligatory by reason, in deference to the Mu'tazilite doctrine. Al-Baydawi did not care for this, so he expressed it in the words he used. Or because the surah comprises the whole of its meanings, from theoretical wisdom and practical rulings, which are the following of the straight path, and the knowledge of the ranks of the blessed and the abodes of the wretched. The first is derived from the beginning of the surah to His saying ﴿Day of Judgement﴾. The second is derived from His saying ﴿You alone we worship﴾ and what follows it. Following the straight path is from His saying ﴿Guide us﴾ and so on. The knowledge comes from His saying ﴿upon whom You have bestowed favour﴾ and so on, and it includes promise and warning, so these are included. Parables and stories, whose purpose is admonition, are likewise. Prayer and praise are likewise. These are the general meanings of the Qur'anic meanings, in correspondence and implication. More detailed than this is to say that it comprises four kinds of knowledge, which are the foundation of religion.

The first is the science of the fundamentals (*'ilm al-usul*), whose core is knowledge of God Most High and His attributes, to which the words ﴿Lord of the worlds﴾ and ﴿the Most Merciful, the Ever-Merciful﴾ point. Also knowledge of the prophethoods, which is meant by His saying ﴿upon whom You have bestowed favour﴾, and the Return, indicated by His saying ﴿Master of the Day of Judgement﴾.

(Second) The science of the branches (*ʿilm al-furūʿ*, the rulings of practical law), whose foundation is the acts of worship. This is what is meant by His saying: ﴿You alone we worship﴾. These acts are both physical and financial, and both depend on the affairs of livelihood, including transactions and marriages, and they necessarily require governance. Thus the branches are built upon the foundations.

(Third) The science of what achieves perfection, which is the science of ethics (*ʿilm al-akhlāq*). Its highest aim is arrival at the Divine Presence (*al-ḥaḍrah al-ṣamadāniyyah*) and travelling the path of uprightness through the stations of those exalted ranks. To this is the allusion in His saying: ﴿You alone we ask for help﴾ and ﴿Guide us to the straight path﴾.

(Fourth) The science of stories and reports about past nations, the happy and the wretched, and what relates to them of promise and warning. This is what is meant by His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿...not of those who have earned anger, nor of those who are astray﴾. If your mind expands, you will arrive at something more expansive than this.

These two aspects require taking the Book as meanings, or estimating those meanings within the *iḍāfī* (genitive) construction. The first aspect does not require this. For this reason some scholars preferred it, though it is subtler and sweeter. It does not create a problem for these two aspects, namely the report that al-Fatiha equals two-thirds of the Qur'an, because that problem is removed once it is established that the summary is not equal to the detail. Thus the increase in its letters, letter by letter, is another third of reward. This was said by al-Shihab. Then he said: "It is strange what has been said here, that this is because it includes the indication of implication (*dalālat al-taḍammun*) and of necessity (*dalālat al-iltizām*), which are two-thirds of the types of indication." End of quote.

I say: More strange than this is his direction, may God have mercy on him, together with what al-Daylami narrated in *al-Firdaws* from Abu al-Darda': "The Opening of the Book (al-Fatiha) suffices for what nothing else in the Qur'an suffices for. If the Opening of the Book were placed on one pan of the scale, and the Qur'an on the other pan, the Opening of the Book would outweigh the Qur'an seven times." For this report does not suggest anything except superiority in reward. Its apparent meaning therefore contradicts that report under his direction, whereas under the direction of the author of the saying there is no contradiction. Yes, it is far-fetched. The two reports can be reconciled, and the difficulty disappears in this way: the first statement was made earlier, and the reward was later multiplied; there is no restriction on the vast mercy. Or: the difference in statement is due to a difference in circumstance. Or: what equals a thing entire equals two-thirds of it. Or: "the Qur'an" in one of the two reports, or in both, means the prayer, as in His saying: ﴿And the recitation of dawn; indeed, the recitation of dawn is ever witnessed﴾. This varies according to the different levels of people in their recitation and their prayers. So let it be reflected upon. In any case, these two (explanations) cannot be measured against what has been said about the reason for its naming in this way: because it is the best of the surahs; or because its sanctity is like the sanctity of the whole Qur'an; or because the refuge of the people of faith is to it; or because it is *muḥkam* (clear and decisive), and the *muḥkamāt* are the "mother of the Book." I do not object to some of these on the basis of non-consistency, because the reason for a name need not be consistent. But I leave the matter to you, and may God's peace be upon you.

(Objection): If al-Fatiha comprises the meanings of the Book, why are seven letters missing from it: *thā'*, *jīm*, *khā'*, *zāy*, *shīn*, *ẓā'*, and *fā'*? We say: Perhaps this is to indicate that perfection in meaning does not require perfection in form, and that its lack of form does not diminish it. Indeed, God, Exalted is He, does not look at your forms. Also, they were seven, corresponding to the number of verses, which contains many secrets. And they were among the dark letters (*al-ḥurūf al-ẓalmāniyyah*) that were not found in the ambiguous openings of the surahs. And after removing the repeated letters, the letters are gathered in the phrase (*ṣirāṭun ʿalā ḥaqqin numsikuh*, "a path upon truth we hold fast"). These are the luminous letters (*al-nūrāniyyah*), all of which are included in al-Fatiha. This indicates the predominance of beauty over majesty, which is suggested by the repetition in al-Fatiha of what points to mercy. The remaining seven of this type were not removed, so that the luminous letters would not be purely luminous; this makes known that the matter is mixed, and none feels secure from the plan of God except the losers. And in His saying: ﴿Inform My servants that I am the Forgiving, the Merciful﴾ and ﴿And that My punishment is the painful punishment﴾, there is an allusion, and what an allusion, to this for whoever reflects on the state of the two sentences. Moreover, in the fact that the luminous letters, which are fourteen, are mentioned in full, while the dark letters are mentioned as seven, and when the units are paired, there results a luminous letter accompanied by a dark one, and a purely luminous one, this is an indication of the two categories of believers: a believer whose light of faith has not been tainted by the darkness of his sins, and a believer who has been mixed with that. In it there is also a symbol that there is no contradiction between faith and disobedience, so the darkness of the latter does not extinguish the light of the former. The hadith "The adulterer does not commit adultery while he is a believer" is to be understood as referring to perfection, and that is not the subject here. When we consider what is omitted, namely the purely dark letters, which indicate the purely wrongdoing (*ẓālim*) who has fallen from the level of consideration, and what is mentioned, namely the purely luminous letters, which indicate the purely believing person, and the mixed luminous letters, which indicate the mixed believer, the secret of the triple division becomes apparent in His saying: ﴿Among them is one who wrongs himself, and among them is one who is moderate, and among them is one who is foremost in good deeds, by permission of God. That is the great bounty﴾. The reason that exactly these seven were omitted from those fourteen, and not the reverse, so that what is affirmed is removed and what is removed is affirmed, or so that seven others derived from this are removed, is due to a secret knowledge, and whoever is ignorant of it is ignorant. Yes, in the fact that the omitted letters are only the dotted ones there is an indication that "the *ghayn* is in the *ʿayn*, and the *rayn* is in between," and therefore the veil has fallen and doubt has arisen. This is what appears to people like us of the secrets of the Book of God, Exalted is He. How far it is from what becomes apparent to the knowers who are immersed in its seas and who have drunk fully from the water of Zamzam of its secrets.

Our master, the scholar Fakhr al-Din al-Razi, has a statement at this point that has no slightest acquaintance with verification. He made the reason for the omission of these letters that they indicate punishment. Thus the *thā'* indicates *thubūr* (perdition), the *jīm* is the first letter of Jahannam, the *khā'* indicates *khizy* (disgrace), and the *zāy* and *shīn* are from *zafīr* (groaning) and *shahīq* (sobbing). Also, the *zāy* indicates *zaqqūm*, the *shīn* indicates *shaqā'* (wretchedness), and the *ẓā'* is the first letter of *ẓill* (shade) in His saying: ﴿Proceed to a shade of three branches﴾. Also it indicates *laẓā*, and the *fā'* indicates *firāq* (separation). Then he said: "If they say: there is no letter except that it is mentioned in the name of something that entails some kind of punishment, then there is no benefit left in what you have mentioned. We say: The benefit in it is that He said about the description of Hell: ﴿It has seven gates; for each gate there is a designated portion﴾. Then, Exalted is He, removed seven letters from this surah, which are the initial words indicating punishment, as a reminder that whoever recites this surah, believes in it, and knows its realities, becomes safe from the seven levels of Hell." End of quote. What is in it is not hidden, and his answer neither benefits him nor suffices him. For someone may say: then let the *dhāl*, *wāw*, *nūn*, *ḥā'*, *ʿayn*, *mīm*, and *ghayn* be omitted as well, since the *wāw* is from *wayl* (woe), the *dhāl* from *dhilla* (humiliation), the *nūn* from *nār* (fire), the *ḥā'* from *ḥamīm* (boiling water), the *ʿayn* from *ʿadhāb* (punishment), the *mīm* from *mihād* (bed/resting place), and the *ghayn* from *ghawāshī* (overwhelming things). The verses are evident, and all of them concern the people of the Fire. The benefit of omitting these would be like the benefit of omitting those, without any difference at all. Moreover, in his words, may God Exalted have mercy on him, there is something other than this. Indeed, even granting that his statement is free from what has been said or may be said, I do not approve of it for Fakhr, who is the master who became the felicity of the religion, the proof of Islam, and the defender of its people.

As for attributing it to the Commander of the Faithful, ʿAlī, may God honour his face, when Caesar of Rome asked Muʿāwiya about this and he did not answer, so he asked ʿAlī and he answered: there is no basis for it. And even on the assumption of its acceptance, what was the Commander's purpose in being content with this measure, except to alert the questioner to secrets that are not hidden from you? So understand this, and may God Exalted take care of your guidance.

(Fifth, sixth, and seventh names): *al-Kanz* (the Treasure), *al-Wāfiyah* (the Sufficient), and *al-Kāfiyah* (the Adequate), because of what has been mentioned about its inclusion of hidden jewels; it suffices and is sufficient. Or because it is not halved in prayer, and nothing else can substitute for it in prayer.

(Eighth): *al-Asās* (the Foundation), because it is the origin of the Qur'an and the first surah in it.

(Ninth, tenth, eleventh, twelfth, and thirteenth): the Surah of Praise, the Surah of Gratitude, the Surah of Supplication, the Surah of Teaching the Request, and the Surah of Asking, because of its inclusion of these. As for its inclusion of praise, it is evident. Likewise gratitude, for whoever has been blessed by God with understanding. It is possible that these names are like "the Mother of the Qur'an" and "the Mother of the Book."

As for its inclusion of the third (ethics), it is like its inclusion of the first, rather more evident. As for teaching the request, it is because it begins with praise before it. The fifth is like the third, and these two are like those two, the third and fourth, as is not hidden.

(Fourteenth and fifteenth): the Surah of Intimate Conversation (*al-munājāh*) and the Surah of Delegation (*al-tafwīd*), because the servant converses with his Lord by saying: ﴿You alone we worship and You alone we ask for help﴾, and by this, delegation is achieved.

(Sixteenth, seventeenth, and eighteenth): the Incantation (*al-ruqyah*), the Cure (*al-shifā'*), and the Healing (*al-shāfiyah*). The authentic hadiths indicate this.

(Nineteenth): the Surah of Prayer, because it is obligatory or a pillar (*farīḍah*) in it. Recommendation is the view of some jurists, and a narration from some regarding voluntary prayer. It has been said: among its names is "the Prayer," based on the hadith: "I have divided the prayer between Me and My servant into two halves." He meant the surah. The linguistic metonymy, by the relation of the whole and the part, or of necessity, actually or by ruling, like the metonymy in ellipsis, is possible.

(Twentieth): *al-Nūr* (the Light), either because it is apparent through its frequent use, or because it illuminates hearts due to the greatness of its rank, or because what it contains of meanings is an expression of the light, meaning the Qur'an.

(Twenty-first): *al-Qur'ān al-ʿAẓīm* (the Great Qur'an), which is evident from what we have previously presented.

(Twenty-second): *al-Sabʿ al-Mathānī* (the Seven Oft-Repeated), because it consists of seven verses by consensus, and we have not seen anything sharing this except "Ara'ayta" (Surah al-Ma'un). The claim that it has eight verses is like the claim that it has nine; it is an anomalous view that does not deserve attention, or it is an error by a narrator. However, some counted the basmala as a verse but not "those upon whom You have bestowed favour," and some did the reverse, and the basis is the transmission. The second opinion is not weakened by the fact that the length of this verse does not correspond to the length of the verse-endings of other surahs. Moreover, in Surah al-Nasr there is something of this kind. It is repeated (*tuthannā*) and repeated (*tukarrar*) in every rak'ah and in every prayer containing bowing. Or the intended meaning is the common and usual meaning of prayer, so a single rak'ah is not objected to, nor is the funeral prayer. Moreover, there is disagreement concerning the *batīrā'* (a prayer without tashahhud), and the funeral prayer is a supplication, not a prayer in the true sense. It has been said that it is described by this because it is repeated (*tuthannā*) with another surah, or because it was revealed twice, or because it is of two kinds: supplication and praise, or because whenever the servant recites one verse of it, God repeats it by reporting His action, as in the well-known hadith. Other statements have also been made. These statements are based on the assumption that *mathānī* comes from *tathniyah* (repetition). It is possible that it comes from *thanā'* (praise), because it contains praise of God, or because of what is reported of praise for whoever recites it. It is also possible that it comes from *thunyā* (exception), because God has singled it out for this Community, and to God belongs praise for this blessing.

Then, the wisdom in the Qur'an being divided into surahs, like books, contrary to al-Zarkashi's view, is that it is more energizing for the reciter and more motivating for acquiring knowledge, like the traveller who, when he covers a mile or a league, refreshes himself by it and becomes energetic for the journey. When the memorizer takes a surah, he believes he has taken from the Book of God a distinct portion, and so what he has memorized becomes great in his eyes. Also, when a genus includes various types and kinds, it is better than if it had only one chapter beneath it. Along with this, there is in it a confirmation that the surah by itself is a miracle and one of the signs of God, Exalted is He. The wisdom in its being long and short is more evident than to be hidden.

**Surat al-Fatiha (The Opening Chapter of the Book)**

Scholars have differed about this surah. Most hold that it is Meccan, and some say it was among the first parts of the Qur'an to be revealed. This is the view narrated from Ali, Ibn Abbas, Qatadah, and most of the Companions. Mujahid alone held that it is Medinan, and this view is regarded as an unusual lapse on his part. It has also been said that it was revealed in Mecca when the prayer was prescribed and in Medina when the *qiblah* (direction of prayer) was changed, so that it would be known that it belongs to the prayer as it was. It has also been said that part of it is Meccan and part Medinan, but the weakness of this view is clear. People have commonly argued for its Meccan origin from the verse of al-Hijr: ﴿And We have certainly given you seven of the oft-repeated [verses] and the Great Qur'an﴾. This is a Meccan surah according to the explicit statement of the scholars and a report from Ibn Abbas. It has the status of a *marfu'* report (one traced back to the Prophet), not because what precedes and follows it concerns the people of Mecca, as has been said, because that rests on the premise that a Meccan revelation is one addressed to the people of Mecca, whereas the well-known view is otherwise. The stronger argument is the transmission from the Companions who witnessed the revelation and descent of the Qur'an, for this rests first on interpreting "the seven oft-repeated" as referring to al-Fatiha. Although this is sound and established in the hadiths, it is also soundly reported from Ibn Abbas and others that it refers to the seven long surahs. Second, the argument rests on the impossibility of bestowing a favour through something before it is given, whereas God Most High has bestowed favours upon Him (ﷺ) before giving them, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, We have granted you a clear victory﴾. This was revealed years before the conquest, and the use of the past tense indicates the certainty of its occurrence. Although this is contrary to the apparent meaning, especially with the presence of the particle *lam* and the word *qad*, and its occurrence in the context of a favour (where the usual sense is that the event has already taken place), and the sequence ﴿And do not strain your eyes toward what We have given to some pairs of them﴾, the argument has nevertheless been challenged. It cannot be said that this and that only indicate that the surah was revealed in Mecca, and not that it was not revealed in Medina, because we reply: negation is the default, and the one who claims affirmation must establish it, and how can he do so? As for what they said in answer to the objection, that descent is the appearance from the unseen world into the visible one, and that appearance in the visible world does not admit of repetition, for the appearance of something apparent is itself manifestly void, like obtaining what is already obtained, based on the claim that it was revealed in each case for a purpose, or that it was revealed in one manner once and another manner another time because of the occurrence of the variant readings *Malik* and *Malik*, or with *Basmalah* at times and without it at others, and the gathering of these views and reports only confirms the occurrence (of revelation in both places) without necessitating it, as is clear.

The surah is written with a hamza and without a hamza, with substitution, if it derives from *su'r*, which means remainder, because the remainder of everything is a part of it. Without the hamza, if it derives from *sur al-bina'* (the wall of a building), which means a station, or *sur al-madinah* (the wall of a city), because it encloses its verses, or from *tasawwur*, which means height and elevation, because it is elevated by being the speech of God Most High. It is also used for a lofty station, as in the words of al-Nabigha:

*Have you not seen that God has given you a surah?*
*You see every angel around it swaying.*

The Qur'an has unified it as one comprising a beginning and an end. It has also been said that it is a distinct section, so that the verse of the Throne (*Ayat al-Kursi*) is excluded, being a distinct verse by tradition. The names of all the surahs are established by hadiths and reports. Whoever holds that it is disliked to say "the surah of such-and-such," but rather "a surah in which such-and-such is mentioned," on the basis of what is reported from Anas and Ibn Umar prohibiting this, is not to be relied upon, since the hadith from Anas is weak or fabricated, and the hadith from Ibn Umar is a statement of his own (*mawquf*), even if it is reported from him with a sound chain.

*Al-Fatihah* is in origin an adjective, given either as the name for the first part of a thing because it is the means of opening the whole, with the *ta'* marking transmission (from adjective to noun) or intensification. It is not restricted to the pattern of a sign or to a verbal noun. It was applied to the first thing by designating the object by the verbal noun, to indicate its primacy, as if it were the very act of opening, since its connection to the opening is first, and then through it the whole collection is connected, being a part of it. The same is said of *al-Khatimah* (the conclusion), for reaching the end first befalls the last part, and the whole is through it. This is not like the first case, because the form *fa'ilah* is rare among verbal nouns. Nevertheless, it is preferable to say that it is not an instrument or a motive, because these are linked to the act and accompany it, and it is generally the case that an instrument does not have the attribute and a motive does not accompany the act. Moreover, the instrumental sense is unsuitable here, since it would imply that some part is not intended. They also permitted it to be an attributive relation, meaning "possessing an opening," along with other less preferred possibilities.

"The Book" is the individual collected whole. The opening of al-Fatihah is in relation to this whole, not to the common concept shared between it and its parts. This is realised in the knowledge, or the Tablet, or the House of Honour (*Bayt al-'Izzah*). There is no harm in the surah being known by this name from early times. The first idiom is the annexation of a name to what it names, which is well known. The second idiom means *li*, the sense of belonging, as in "a part of a thing," not *min* (of), as in "a ring of silver," because the annexed term is partial. This was said by Shaykh al-Islam, and it is the view of some concerning all such cases. Ibn Kaysan and al-Sirafi said that the annexation of a part is in the sense of the partitive *min*. In the *Lumma'* and its commentary it is said that *min* implied in annexation is in general of this kind, without distinguishing between a part and a partial term. Some made the annexation of a partial term explanatory in all cases, and some restricted it to a relation of general and specific overlap, as in the example, and made it a *lam* relation in the absolute case, like "the city of Baghdad." The common usage does not support this.

This noble surah has names which some have counted at over twenty. One of them is *Fatihat al-Kitab* (The Opening of the Book), because it is the beginning of the Book in its known order, not because it is recited at the beginning of teaching or the recitation in prayer, as the Imam al-Suyuti supposed, nor because it was the first surah revealed, as has been said. As for the first and third names, the priority in terms of teaching or revelation requires observing the order in the rest of the parts of the Book from those two aspects. There is no doubt that the order of teaching and the order of revelation are not like the known order. As for the second name, you know that the meaning of "the Book" is not the common concept applying to what is recited in prayer, so that its priority to it would be considered in the naming. Al-Mursi related that it was called this because it is the first surah written on the Tablet. This needs transmission. Even if we affirm that the order of the Qur'an in our codices is as in the Tablet, it may be that the follower was written and then the one followed was written. Strong probability is a separate matter.

The second name is *Fatihat al-Qur'an* (The Opening of the Qur'an), for the reason we have already mentioned, exactly in the same manner.

The third and fourth names are *Umm al-Kitab* (The Mother of the Book) and *Umm al-Qur'an* (The Mother of the Qur'an). The hadith "Let none of you say *Umm al-Kitab*; let him say *Fatihat al-Kitab*" has no basis. Indeed, its being named this is established in the sound collections, as will not be hidden from one who examines them. It was named this because the beginning, whether in writing, recitation, or descent according to one view, or in prayer with it, and what follows it is a follower of it. So it is like the mother upon whom the child is formed afterwards. The word *umm* is also used for a standard, because it precedes and the army follows it, and from this comes *Umm al-Qura* (the Mother of Cities). Or because it comprises, as the scholar (*al-'Allamah*) said, the principal meanings in the Qur'an: praise of God Most High with what He is worthy of, worship through command and prohibition, and warning. As for praise, it is obvious. As for worship, it arises either from ﴿Praise be to God﴾, because it is for teaching, so a command is implied which it conveys, and the affirmative command necessarily entails a generic prohibition of its opposite, which we do not regard as objectionable. Or from ﴿Guide us to the straight path﴾, if by it is meant the religion of Islam. Or from the supposition "Say: In the name of God," with its complement delayed. As for worship from ﴿You alone we worship﴾, it is an announcement of its exclusive devotion to worship, which is the realisation of servanthood by carrying out what the Master commands or forbids. This indicates in general that they are obliged to worship. It is not objected against the Mu'tazilah (a rationalist theological school) that there was no prior command or prohibition at all. We answer, once the absence of prior command is granted, that the foundation of worship is monotheism, and the opening suggests this. Especially since the Prophet (ﷺ) was already charged with monotheism and conveying the surah, and this suffices. As for promise and warning, they come from God Most High's words ﴿the way of those upon whom You have bestowed favour, not of those who have incurred wrath﴾, or from ﴿the Day of Judgement﴾, meaning the recompense. What is recompensed is either what gladdens or what harms, namely reward and punishment. These purposes apply because the sending of messengers and the revelation of books are a mercy to the servants and guidance towards what sets their lives and their final returns right. This is achieved by knowing who is able to bring blessings into being, and sustain them, and then by reaching Him through what binds what is present, draws more, and in practice and belief, and by freeing oneself from what leads to losing what has been gained and prevents what has been obtained, in heart and body. Praise is the branch of knowing the one praised together with his deserving it. This includes knowledge of the attributes of majesty and beauty, among which are those by which messengers are sent and books revealed, and the difference between the obedient and the sinner. Thus belief in God Most High, His attributes, the prophethood, and the Return enters in general. Worship is made possible by these, and in it enters, by way of belief, the prophethood and what relates to it, including the Book and the angels, since command and prohibition are a branch of the established truth of these in general. Promise and warning imply belief in the Return and stir one to worship. People are like a hundred camels, among which you find no riding camel. Most are moved by desire and fear, the middling ones by hope and dread, and the elect, though few, by intimacy and awe. By these three the guidance to the interests of this life and the next is complete. I do not confine for you the way of restriction to this, for the path of the mind has room. You may reduce the three to two, by including praise within worship, since the mind has no judgement. Perhaps he (al-Zamakhshari) made it a separate division from it as a hint that gratitude to the Benefactor is obligatory by reason, in deference to the Mu'tazilite doctrine. Al-Baydawi did not care for this, so he expressed it in the words he used. Or because the surah comprises the whole of its meanings, from theoretical wisdom and practical rulings, which are the following of the straight path, and the knowledge of the ranks of the blessed and the abodes of the wretched. The first is derived from the beginning of the surah to His saying ﴿Day of Judgement﴾. The second is derived from His saying ﴿You alone we worship﴾ and what follows it. Following the straight path is from His saying ﴿Guide us﴾ and so on. The knowledge comes from His saying ﴿upon whom You have bestowed favour﴾ and so on, and it includes promise and warning, so these are included. Parables and stories, whose purpose is admonition, are likewise. Prayer and praise are likewise. These are the general meanings of the Qur'anic meanings, in correspondence and implication. More detailed than this is to say that it comprises four kinds of knowledge, which are the foundation of religion.

The first is the science of the fundamentals (*'ilm al-usul*), whose core is knowledge of God Most High and His attributes, to which the words ﴿Lord of the worlds﴾ and ﴿the Most Merciful, the Ever-Merciful﴾ point. Also knowledge of the prophethoods, which is meant by His saying ﴿upon whom You have bestowed favour﴾, and the Return, indicated by His saying ﴿Master of the Day of Judgement﴾.

(Second) The science of the branches (*ʿilm al-furūʿ*, the rulings of practical law), whose foundation is the acts of worship. This is what is meant by His saying: ﴿You alone we worship﴾. These acts are both physical and financial, and both depend on the affairs of livelihood, including transactions and marriages, and they necessarily require governance. Thus the branches are built upon the foundations.

(Third) The science of what achieves perfection, which is the science of ethics (*ʿilm al-akhlāq*). Its highest aim is arrival at the Divine Presence (*al-ḥaḍrah al-ṣamadāniyyah*) and travelling the path of uprightness through the stations of those exalted ranks. To this is the allusion in His saying: ﴿You alone we ask for help﴾ and ﴿Guide us to the straight path﴾.

(Fourth) The science of stories and reports about past nations, the happy and the wretched, and what relates to them of promise and warning. This is what is meant by His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿...not of those who have earned anger, nor of those who are astray﴾. If your mind expands, you will arrive at something more expansive than this.

These two aspects require taking the Book as meanings, or estimating those meanings within the *iḍāfī* (genitive) construction. The first aspect does not require this. For this reason some scholars preferred it, though it is subtler and sweeter. It does not create a problem for these two aspects, namely the report that al-Fatiha equals two-thirds of the Qur'an, because that problem is removed once it is established that the summary is not equal to the detail. Thus the increase in its letters, letter by letter, is another third of reward. This was said by al-Shihab. Then he said: "It is strange what has been said here, that this is because it includes the indication of implication (*dalālat al-taḍammun*) and of necessity (*dalālat al-iltizām*), which are two-thirds of the types of indication." End of quote.

I say: More strange than this is his direction, may God have mercy on him, together with what al-Daylami narrated in *al-Firdaws* from Abu al-Darda': "The Opening of the Book (al-Fatiha) suffices for what nothing else in the Qur'an suffices for. If the Opening of the Book were placed on one pan of the scale, and the Qur'an on the other pan, the Opening of the Book would outweigh the Qur'an seven times." For this report does not suggest anything except superiority in reward. Its apparent meaning therefore contradicts that report under his direction, whereas under the direction of the author of the saying there is no contradiction. Yes, it is far-fetched. The two reports can be reconciled, and the difficulty disappears in this way: the first statement was made earlier, and the reward was later multiplied; there is no restriction on the vast mercy. Or: the difference in statement is due to a difference in circumstance. Or: what equals a thing entire equals two-thirds of it. Or: "the Qur'an" in one of the two reports, or in both, means the prayer, as in His saying: ﴿And the recitation of dawn; indeed, the recitation of dawn is ever witnessed﴾. This varies according to the different levels of people in their recitation and their prayers. So let it be reflected upon. In any case, these two (explanations) cannot be measured against what has been said about the reason for its naming in this way: because it is the best of the surahs; or because its sanctity is like the sanctity of the whole Qur'an; or because the refuge of the people of faith is to it; or because it is *muḥkam* (clear and decisive), and the *muḥkamāt* are the "mother of the Book." I do not object to some of these on the basis of non-consistency, because the reason for a name need not be consistent. But I leave the matter to you, and may God's peace be upon you.

(Objection): If al-Fatiha comprises the meanings of the Book, why are seven letters missing from it: *thā'*, *jīm*, *khā'*, *zāy*, *shīn*, *ẓā'*, and *fā'*? We say: Perhaps this is to indicate that perfection in meaning does not require perfection in form, and that its lack of form does not diminish it. Indeed, God, Exalted is He, does not look at your forms. Also, they were seven, corresponding to the number of verses, which contains many secrets. And they were among the dark letters (*al-ḥurūf al-ẓalmāniyyah*) that were not found in the ambiguous openings of the surahs. And after removing the repeated letters, the letters are gathered in the phrase (*ṣirāṭun ʿalā ḥaqqin numsikuh*, "a path upon truth we hold fast"). These are the luminous letters (*al-nūrāniyyah*), all of which are included in al-Fatiha. This indicates the predominance of beauty over majesty, which is suggested by the repetition in al-Fatiha of what points to mercy. The remaining seven of this type were not removed, so that the luminous letters would not be purely luminous; this makes known that the matter is mixed, and none feels secure from the plan of God except the losers. And in His saying: ﴿Inform My servants that I am the Forgiving, the Merciful﴾ and ﴿And that My punishment is the painful punishment﴾, there is an allusion, and what an allusion, to this for whoever reflects on the state of the two sentences. Moreover, in the fact that the luminous letters, which are fourteen, are mentioned in full, while the dark letters are mentioned as seven, and when the units are paired, there results a luminous letter accompanied by a dark one, and a purely luminous one, this is an indication of the two categories of believers: a believer whose light of faith has not been tainted by the darkness of his sins, and a believer who has been mixed with that. In it there is also a symbol that there is no contradiction between faith and disobedience, so the darkness of the latter does not extinguish the light of the former. The hadith "The adulterer does not commit adultery while he is a believer" is to be understood as referring to perfection, and that is not the subject here. When we consider what is omitted, namely the purely dark letters, which indicate the purely wrongdoing (*ẓālim*) who has fallen from the level of consideration, and what is mentioned, namely the purely luminous letters, which indicate the purely believing person, and the mixed luminous letters, which indicate the mixed believer, the secret of the triple division becomes apparent in His saying: ﴿Among them is one who wrongs himself, and among them is one who is moderate, and among them is one who is foremost in good deeds, by permission of God. That is the great bounty﴾. The reason that exactly these seven were omitted from those fourteen, and not the reverse, so that what is affirmed is removed and what is removed is affirmed, or so that seven others derived from this are removed, is due to a secret knowledge, and whoever is ignorant of it is ignorant. Yes, in the fact that the omitted letters are only the dotted ones there is an indication that "the *ghayn* is in the *ʿayn*, and the *rayn* is in between," and therefore the veil has fallen and doubt has arisen. This is what appears to people like us of the secrets of the Book of God, Exalted is He. How far it is from what becomes apparent to the knowers who are immersed in its seas and who have drunk fully from the water of Zamzam of its secrets.

Our master, the scholar Fakhr al-Din al-Razi, has a statement at this point that has no slightest acquaintance with verification. He made the reason for the omission of these letters that they indicate punishment. Thus the *thā'* indicates *thubūr* (perdition), the *jīm* is the first letter of Jahannam, the *khā'* indicates *khizy* (disgrace), and the *zāy* and *shīn* are from *zafīr* (groaning) and *shahīq* (sobbing). Also, the *zāy* indicates *zaqqūm*, the *shīn* indicates *shaqā'* (wretchedness), and the *ẓā'* is the first letter of *ẓill* (shade) in His saying: ﴿Proceed to a shade of three branches﴾. Also it indicates *laẓā*, and the *fā'* indicates *firāq* (separation). Then he said: "If they say: there is no letter except that it is mentioned in the name of something that entails some kind of punishment, then there is no benefit left in what you have mentioned. We say: The benefit in it is that He said about the description of Hell: ﴿It has seven gates; for each gate there is a designated portion﴾. Then, Exalted is He, removed seven letters from this surah, which are the initial words indicating punishment, as a reminder that whoever recites this surah, believes in it, and knows its realities, becomes safe from the seven levels of Hell." End of quote. What is in it is not hidden, and his answer neither benefits him nor suffices him. For someone may say: then let the *dhāl*, *wāw*, *nūn*, *ḥā'*, *ʿayn*, *mīm*, and *ghayn* be omitted as well, since the *wāw* is from *wayl* (woe), the *dhāl* from *dhilla* (humiliation), the *nūn* from *nār* (fire), the *ḥā'* from *ḥamīm* (boiling water), the *ʿayn* from *ʿadhāb* (punishment), the *mīm* from *mihād* (bed/resting place), and the *ghayn* from *ghawāshī* (overwhelming things). The verses are evident, and all of them concern the people of the Fire. The benefit of omitting these would be like the benefit of omitting those, without any difference at all. Moreover, in his words, may God Exalted have mercy on him, there is something other than this. Indeed, even granting that his statement is free from what has been said or may be said, I do not approve of it for Fakhr, who is the master who became the felicity of the religion, the proof of Islam, and the defender of its people.

As for attributing it to the Commander of the Faithful, ʿAlī, may God honour his face, when Caesar of Rome asked Muʿāwiya about this and he did not answer, so he asked ʿAlī and he answered: there is no basis for it. And even on the assumption of its acceptance, what was the Commander's purpose in being content with this measure, except to alert the questioner to secrets that are not hidden from you? So understand this, and may God Exalted take care of your guidance.

(Fifth, sixth, and seventh names): *al-Kanz* (the Treasure), *al-Wāfiyah* (the Sufficient), and *al-Kāfiyah* (the Adequate), because of what has been mentioned about its inclusion of hidden jewels; it suffices and is sufficient. Or because it is not halved in prayer, and nothing else can substitute for it in prayer.

(Eighth): *al-Asās* (the Foundation), because it is the origin of the Qur'an and the first surah in it.

(Ninth, tenth, eleventh, twelfth, and thirteenth): the Surah of Praise, the Surah of Gratitude, the Surah of Supplication, the Surah of Teaching the Request, and the Surah of Asking, because of its inclusion of these. As for its inclusion of praise, it is evident. Likewise gratitude, for whoever has been blessed by God with understanding. It is possible that these names are like "the Mother of the Qur'an" and "the Mother of the Book."

As for its inclusion of the third (ethics), it is like its inclusion of the first, rather more evident. As for teaching the request, it is because it begins with praise before it. The fifth is like the third, and these two are like those two, the third and fourth, as is not hidden.

(Fourteenth and fifteenth): the Surah of Intimate Conversation (*al-munājāh*) and the Surah of Delegation (*al-tafwīd*), because the servant converses with his Lord by saying: ﴿You alone we worship and You alone we ask for help﴾, and by this, delegation is achieved.

(Sixteenth, seventeenth, and eighteenth): the Incantation (*al-ruqyah*), the Cure (*al-shifā'*), and the Healing (*al-shāfiyah*). The authentic hadiths indicate this.

(Nineteenth): the Surah of Prayer, because it is obligatory or a pillar (*farīḍah*) in it. Recommendation is the view of some jurists, and a narration from some regarding voluntary prayer. It has been said: among its names is "the Prayer," based on the hadith: "I have divided the prayer between Me and My servant into two halves." He meant the surah. The linguistic metonymy, by the relation of the whole and the part, or of necessity, actually or by ruling, like the metonymy in ellipsis, is possible.

(Twentieth): *al-Nūr* (the Light), either because it is apparent through its frequent use, or because it illuminates hearts due to the greatness of its rank, or because what it contains of meanings is an expression of the light, meaning the Qur'an.

(Twenty-first): *al-Qur'ān al-ʿAẓīm* (the Great Qur'an), which is evident from what we have previously presented.

(Twenty-second): *al-Sabʿ al-Mathānī* (the Seven Oft-Repeated), because it consists of seven verses by consensus, and we have not seen anything sharing this except "Ara'ayta" (Surah al-Ma'un). The claim that it has eight verses is like the claim that it has nine; it is an anomalous view that does not deserve attention, or it is an error by a narrator. However, some counted the basmala as a verse but not "those upon whom You have bestowed favour," and some did the reverse, and the basis is the transmission. The second opinion is not weakened by the fact that the length of this verse does not correspond to the length of the verse-endings of other surahs. Moreover, in Surah al-Nasr there is something of this kind. It is repeated (*tuthannā*) and repeated (*tukarrar*) in every rak'ah and in every prayer containing bowing. Or the intended meaning is the common and usual meaning of prayer, so a single rak'ah is not objected to, nor is the funeral prayer. Moreover, there is disagreement concerning the *batīrā'* (a prayer without tashahhud), and the funeral prayer is a supplication, not a prayer in the true sense. It has been said that it is described by this because it is repeated (*tuthannā*) with another surah, or because it was revealed twice, or because it is of two kinds: supplication and praise, or because whenever the servant recites one verse of it, God repeats it by reporting His action, as in the well-known hadith. Other statements have also been made. These statements are based on the assumption that *mathānī* comes from *tathniyah* (repetition). It is possible that it comes from *thanā'* (praise), because it contains praise of God, or because of what is reported of praise for whoever recites it. It is also possible that it comes from *thunyā* (exception), because God has singled it out for this Community, and to God belongs praise for this blessing.

Then, the wisdom in the Qur'an being divided into surahs, like books, contrary to al-Zarkashi's view, is that it is more energizing for the reciter and more motivating for acquiring knowledge, like the traveller who, when he covers a mile or a league, refreshes himself by it and becomes energetic for the journey. When the memorizer takes a surah, he believes he has taken from the Book of God a distinct portion, and so what he has memorized becomes great in his eyes. Also, when a genus includes various types and kinds, it is better than if it had only one chapter beneath it. Along with this, there is in it a confirmation that the surah by itself is a miracle and one of the signs of God, Exalted is He. The wisdom in its being long and short is more evident than to be hidden.

**Surat al-Fatiha (The Opening Chapter of the Book)**

Scholars have differed about this surah. Most hold that it is Meccan, and some say it was among the first parts of the Qur'an to be revealed. This is the view narrated from Ali, Ibn Abbas, Qatadah, and most of the Companions. Mujahid alone held that it is Medinan, and this view is regarded as an unusual lapse on his part. It has also been said that it was revealed in Mecca when the prayer was prescribed and in Medina when the *qiblah* (direction of prayer) was changed, so that it would be known that it belongs to the prayer as it was. It has also been said that part of it is Meccan and part Medinan, but the weakness of this view is clear. People have commonly argued for its Meccan origin from the verse of al-Hijr: ﴿And We have certainly given you seven of the oft-repeated [verses] and the Great Qur'an﴾. This is a Meccan surah according to the explicit statement of the scholars and a report from Ibn Abbas. It has the status of a *marfu'* report (one traced back to the Prophet), not because what precedes and follows it concerns the people of Mecca, as has been said, because that rests on the premise that a Meccan revelation is one addressed to the people of Mecca, whereas the well-known view is otherwise. The stronger argument is the transmission from the Companions who witnessed the revelation and descent of the Qur'an, for this rests first on interpreting "the seven oft-repeated" as referring to al-Fatiha. Although this is sound and established in the hadiths, it is also soundly reported from Ibn Abbas and others that it refers to the seven long surahs. Second, the argument rests on the impossibility of bestowing a favour through something before it is given, whereas God Most High has bestowed favours upon Him (ﷺ) before giving them, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, We have granted you a clear victory﴾. This was revealed years before the conquest, and the use of the past tense indicates the certainty of its occurrence. Although this is contrary to the apparent meaning, especially with the presence of the particle *lam* and the word *qad*, and its occurrence in the context of a favour (where the usual sense is that the event has already taken place), and the sequence ﴿And do not strain your eyes toward what We have given to some pairs of them﴾, the argument has nevertheless been challenged. It cannot be said that this and that only indicate that the surah was revealed in Mecca, and not that it was not revealed in Medina, because we reply: negation is the default, and the one who claims affirmation must establish it, and how can he do so? As for what they said in answer to the objection, that descent is the appearance from the unseen world into the visible one, and that appearance in the visible world does not admit of repetition, for the appearance of something apparent is itself manifestly void, like obtaining what is already obtained, based on the claim that it was revealed in each case for a purpose, or that it was revealed in one manner once and another manner another time because of the occurrence of the variant readings *Malik* and *Malik*, or with *Basmalah* at times and without it at others, and the gathering of these views and reports only confirms the occurrence (of revelation in both places) without necessitating it, as is clear.

The surah is written with a hamza and without a hamza, with substitution, if it derives from *su'r*, which means remainder, because the remainder of everything is a part of it. Without the hamza, if it derives from *sur al-bina'* (the wall of a building), which means a station, or *sur al-madinah* (the wall of a city), because it encloses its verses, or from *tasawwur*, which means height and elevation, because it is elevated by being the speech of God Most High. It is also used for a lofty station, as in the words of al-Nabigha:

*Have you not seen that God has given you a surah?*
*You see every angel around it swaying.*

The Qur'an has unified it as one comprising a beginning and an end. It has also been said that it is a distinct section, so that the verse of the Throne (*Ayat al-Kursi*) is excluded, being a distinct verse by tradition. The names of all the surahs are established by hadiths and reports. Whoever holds that it is disliked to say "the surah of such-and-such," but rather "a surah in which such-and-such is mentioned," on the basis of what is reported from Anas and Ibn Umar prohibiting this, is not to be relied upon, since the hadith from Anas is weak or fabricated, and the hadith from Ibn Umar is a statement of his own (*mawquf*), even if it is reported from him with a sound chain.

*Al-Fatihah* is in origin an adjective, given either as the name for the first part of a thing because it is the means of opening the whole, with the *ta'* marking transmission (from adjective to noun) or intensification. It is not restricted to the pattern of a sign or to a verbal noun. It was applied to the first thing by designating the object by the verbal noun, to indicate its primacy, as if it were the very act of opening, since its connection to the opening is first, and then through it the whole collection is connected, being a part of it. The same is said of *al-Khatimah* (the conclusion), for reaching the end first befalls the last part, and the whole is through it. This is not like the first case, because the form *fa'ilah* is rare among verbal nouns. Nevertheless, it is preferable to say that it is not an instrument or a motive, because these are linked to the act and accompany it, and it is generally the case that an instrument does not have the attribute and a motive does not accompany the act. Moreover, the instrumental sense is unsuitable here, since it would imply that some part is not intended. They also permitted it to be an attributive relation, meaning "possessing an opening," along with other less preferred possibilities.

"The Book" is the individual collected whole. The opening of al-Fatihah is in relation to this whole, not to the common concept shared between it and its parts. This is realised in the knowledge, or the Tablet, or the House of Honour (*Bayt al-'Izzah*). There is no harm in the surah being known by this name from early times. The first idiom is the annexation of a name to what it names, which is well known. The second idiom means *li*, the sense of belonging, as in "a part of a thing," not *min* (of), as in "a ring of silver," because the annexed term is partial. This was said by Shaykh al-Islam, and it is the view of some concerning all such cases. Ibn Kaysan and al-Sirafi said that the annexation of a part is in the sense of the partitive *min*. In the *Lumma'* and its commentary it is said that *min* implied in annexation is in general of this kind, without distinguishing between a part and a partial term. Some made the annexation of a partial term explanatory in all cases, and some restricted it to a relation of general and specific overlap, as in the example, and made it a *lam* relation in the absolute case, like "the city of Baghdad." The common usage does not support this.

This noble surah has names which some have counted at over twenty. One of them is *Fatihat al-Kitab* (The Opening of the Book), because it is the beginning of the Book in its known order, not because it is recited at the beginning of teaching or the recitation in prayer, as the Imam al-Suyuti supposed, nor because it was the first surah revealed, as has been said. As for the first and third names, the priority in terms of teaching or revelation requires observing the order in the rest of the parts of the Book from those two aspects. There is no doubt that the order of teaching and the order of revelation are not like the known order. As for the second name, you know that the meaning of "the Book" is not the common concept applying to what is recited in prayer, so that its priority to it would be considered in the naming. Al-Mursi related that it was called this because it is the first surah written on the Tablet. This needs transmission. Even if we affirm that the order of the Qur'an in our codices is as in the Tablet, it may be that the follower was written and then the one followed was written. Strong probability is a separate matter.

The second name is *Fatihat al-Qur'an* (The Opening of the Qur'an), for the reason we have already mentioned, exactly in the same manner.

The third and fourth names are *Umm al-Kitab* (The Mother of the Book) and *Umm al-Qur'an* (The Mother of the Qur'an). The hadith "Let none of you say *Umm al-Kitab*; let him say *Fatihat al-Kitab*" has no basis. Indeed, its being named this is established in the sound collections, as will not be hidden from one who examines them. It was named this because the beginning, whether in writing, recitation, or descent according to one view, or in prayer with it, and what follows it is a follower of it. So it is like the mother upon whom the child is formed afterwards. The word *umm* is also used for a standard, because it precedes and the army follows it, and from this comes *Umm al-Qura* (the Mother of Cities). Or because it comprises, as the scholar (*al-'Allamah*) said, the principal meanings in the Qur'an: praise of God Most High with what He is worthy of, worship through command and prohibition, and warning. As for praise, it is obvious. As for worship, it arises either from ﴿Praise be to God﴾, because it is for teaching, so a command is implied which it conveys, and the affirmative command necessarily entails a generic prohibition of its opposite, which we do not regard as objectionable. Or from ﴿Guide us to the straight path﴾, if by it is meant the religion of Islam. Or from the supposition "Say: In the name of God," with its complement delayed. As for worship from ﴿You alone we worship﴾, it is an announcement of its exclusive devotion to worship, which is the realisation of servanthood by carrying out what the Master commands or forbids. This indicates in general that they are obliged to worship. It is not objected against the Mu'tazilah (a rationalist theological school) that there was no prior command or prohibition at all. We answer, once the absence of prior command is granted, that the foundation of worship is monotheism, and the opening suggests this. Especially since the Prophet (ﷺ) was already charged with monotheism and conveying the surah, and this suffices. As for promise and warning, they come from God Most High's words ﴿the way of those upon whom You have bestowed favour, not of those who have incurred wrath﴾, or from ﴿the Day of Judgement﴾, meaning the recompense. What is recompensed is either what gladdens or what harms, namely reward and punishment. These purposes apply because the sending of messengers and the revelation of books are a mercy to the servants and guidance towards what sets their lives and their final returns right. This is achieved by knowing who is able to bring blessings into being, and sustain them, and then by reaching Him through what binds what is present, draws more, and in practice and belief, and by freeing oneself from what leads to losing what has been gained and prevents what has been obtained, in heart and body. Praise is the branch of knowing the one praised together with his deserving it. This includes knowledge of the attributes of majesty and beauty, among which are those by which messengers are sent and books revealed, and the difference between the obedient and the sinner. Thus belief in God Most High, His attributes, the prophethood, and the Return enters in general. Worship is made possible by these, and in it enters, by way of belief, the prophethood and what relates to it, including the Book and the angels, since command and prohibition are a branch of the established truth of these in general. Promise and warning imply belief in the Return and stir one to worship. People are like a hundred camels, among which you find no riding camel. Most are moved by desire and fear, the middling ones by hope and dread, and the elect, though few, by intimacy and awe. By these three the guidance to the interests of this life and the next is complete. I do not confine for you the way of restriction to this, for the path of the mind has room. You may reduce the three to two, by including praise within worship, since the mind has no judgement. Perhaps he (al-Zamakhshari) made it a separate division from it as a hint that gratitude to the Benefactor is obligatory by reason, in deference to the Mu'tazilite doctrine. Al-Baydawi did not care for this, so he expressed it in the words he used. Or because the surah comprises the whole of its meanings, from theoretical wisdom and practical rulings, which are the following of the straight path, and the knowledge of the ranks of the blessed and the abodes of the wretched. The first is derived from the beginning of the surah to His saying ﴿Day of Judgement﴾. The second is derived from His saying ﴿You alone we worship﴾ and what follows it. Following the straight path is from His saying ﴿Guide us﴾ and so on. The knowledge comes from His saying ﴿upon whom You have bestowed favour﴾ and so on, and it includes promise and warning, so these are included. Parables and stories, whose purpose is admonition, are likewise. Prayer and praise are likewise. These are the general meanings of the Qur'anic meanings, in correspondence and implication. More detailed than this is to say that it comprises four kinds of knowledge, which are the foundation of religion.

The first is the science of the fundamentals (*'ilm al-usul*), whose core is knowledge of God Most High and His attributes, to which the words ﴿Lord of the worlds﴾ and ﴿the Most Merciful, the Ever-Merciful﴾ point. Also knowledge of the prophethoods, which is meant by His saying ﴿upon whom You have bestowed favour﴾, and the Return, indicated by His saying ﴿Master of the Day of Judgement﴾.

(Second) The science of the branches (*ʿilm al-furūʿ*, the rulings of practical law), whose foundation is the acts of worship. This is what is meant by His saying: ﴿You alone we worship﴾. These acts are both physical and financial, and both depend on the affairs of livelihood, including transactions and marriages, and they necessarily require governance. Thus the branches are built upon the foundations.

(Third) The science of what achieves perfection, which is the science of ethics (*ʿilm al-akhlāq*). Its highest aim is arrival at the Divine Presence (*al-ḥaḍrah al-ṣamadāniyyah*) and travelling the path of uprightness through the stations of those exalted ranks. To this is the allusion in His saying: ﴿You alone we ask for help﴾ and ﴿Guide us to the straight path﴾.

(Fourth) The science of stories and reports about past nations, the happy and the wretched, and what relates to them of promise and warning.
