This is what is meant by His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿...not of those who have earned anger, nor of those who are astray﴾. If your mind expands, you will arrive at something more expansive than this.

These two aspects require taking the Book as meanings, or estimating those meanings within the *iḍāfī* (genitive) construction. The first aspect does not require this. For this reason some scholars preferred it, though it is subtler and sweeter. It does not create a problem for these two aspects, namely the report that al-Fatiha equals two-thirds of the Qur'an, because that problem is removed once it is established that the summary is not equal to the detail. Thus the increase in its letters, letter by letter, is another third of reward. This was said by al-Shihab. Then he said: "It is strange what has been said here, that this is because it includes the indication of implication (*dalālat al-taḍammun*) and of necessity (*dalālat al-iltizām*), which are two-thirds of the types of indication." End of quote.

I say: More strange than this is his direction, may God have mercy on him, together with what al-Daylami narrated in *al-Firdaws* from Abu al-Darda': "The Opening of the Book (al-Fatiha) suffices for what nothing else in the Qur'an suffices for. If the Opening of the Book were placed on one pan of the scale, and the Qur'an on the other pan, the Opening of the Book would outweigh the Qur'an seven times." For this report does not suggest anything except superiority in reward. Its apparent meaning therefore contradicts that report under his direction, whereas under the direction of the author of the saying there is no contradiction. Yes, it is far-fetched. The two reports can be reconciled, and the difficulty disappears in this way: the first statement was made earlier, and the reward was later multiplied; there is no restriction on the vast mercy. Or: the difference in statement is due to a difference in circumstance. Or: what equals a thing entire equals two-thirds of it. Or: "the Qur'an" in one of the two reports, or in both, means the prayer, as in His saying: ﴿And the recitation of dawn; indeed, the recitation of dawn is ever witnessed﴾. This varies according to the different levels of people in their recitation and their prayers. So let it be reflected upon. In any case, these two (explanations) cannot be measured against what has been said about the reason for its naming in this way: because it is the best of the surahs; or because its sanctity is like the sanctity of the whole Qur'an; or because the refuge of the people of faith is to it; or because it is *muḥkam* (clear and decisive), and the *muḥkamāt* are the "mother of the Book." I do not object to some of these on the basis of non-consistency, because the reason for a name need not be consistent. But I leave the matter to you, and may God's peace be upon you.

(Objection): If al-Fatiha comprises the meanings of the Book, why are seven letters missing from it: *thā'*, *jīm*, *khā'*, *zāy*, *shīn*, *ẓā'*, and *fā'*? We say: Perhaps this is to indicate that perfection in meaning does not require perfection in form, and that its lack of form does not diminish it. Indeed, God, Exalted is He, does not look at your forms. Also, they were seven, corresponding to the number of verses, which contains many secrets. And they were among the dark letters (*al-ḥurūf al-ẓalmāniyyah*) that were not found in the ambiguous openings of the surahs. And after removing the repeated letters, the letters are gathered in the phrase (*ṣirāṭun ʿalā ḥaqqin numsikuh*, "a path upon truth we hold fast"). These are the luminous letters (*al-nūrāniyyah*), all of which are included in al-Fatiha. This indicates the predominance of beauty over majesty, which is suggested by the repetition in al-Fatiha of what points to mercy. The remaining seven of this type were not removed, so that the luminous letters would not be purely luminous; this makes known that the matter is mixed, and none feels secure from the plan of God except the losers. And in His saying: ﴿Inform My servants that I am the Forgiving, the Merciful﴾ and ﴿And that My punishment is the painful punishment﴾, there is an allusion, and what an allusion, to this for whoever reflects on the state of the two sentences. Moreover, in the fact that the luminous letters, which are fourteen, are mentioned in full, while the dark letters are mentioned as seven, and when the units are paired, there results a luminous letter accompanied by a dark one, and a purely luminous one, this is an indication of the two categories of believers: a believer whose light of faith has not been tainted by the darkness of his sins, and a believer who has been mixed with that. In it there is also a symbol that there is no contradiction between faith and disobedience, so the darkness of the latter does not extinguish the light of the former. The hadith "The adulterer does not commit adultery while he is a believer" is to be understood as referring to perfection, and that is not the subject here. When we consider what is omitted, namely the purely dark letters, which indicate the purely wrongdoing (*ẓālim*) who has fallen from the level of consideration, and what is mentioned, namely the purely luminous letters, which indicate the purely believing person, and the mixed luminous letters, which indicate the mixed believer, the secret of the triple division becomes apparent in His saying: ﴿Among them is one who wrongs himself, and among them is one who is moderate, and among them is one who is foremost in good deeds, by permission of God. That is the great bounty﴾. The reason that exactly these seven were omitted from those fourteen, and not the reverse, so that what is affirmed is removed and what is removed is affirmed, or so that seven others derived from this are removed, is due to a secret knowledge, and whoever is ignorant of it is ignorant. Yes, in the fact that the omitted letters are only the dotted ones there is an indication that "the *ghayn* is in the *ʿayn*, and the *rayn* is in between," and therefore the veil has fallen and doubt has arisen. This is what appears to people like us of the secrets of the Book of God, Exalted is He. How far it is from what becomes apparent to the knowers who are immersed in its seas and who have drunk fully from the water of Zamzam of its secrets.

Our master, the scholar Fakhr al-Din al-Razi, has a statement at this point that has no slightest acquaintance with verification. He made the reason for the omission of these letters that they indicate punishment. Thus the *thā'* indicates *thubūr* (perdition), the *jīm* is the first letter of Jahannam, the *khā'* indicates *khizy* (disgrace), and the *zāy* and *shīn* are from *zafīr* (groaning) and *shahīq* (sobbing). Also, the *zāy* indicates *zaqqūm*, the *shīn* indicates *shaqā'* (wretchedness), and the *ẓā'* is the first letter of *ẓill* (shade) in His saying: ﴿Proceed to a shade of three branches﴾. Also it indicates *laẓā*, and the *fā'* indicates *firāq* (separation). Then he said: "If they say: there is no letter except that it is mentioned in the name of something that entails some kind of punishment, then there is no benefit left in what you have mentioned. We say: The benefit in it is that He said about the description of Hell: ﴿It has seven gates; for each gate there is a designated portion﴾. Then, Exalted is He, removed seven letters from this surah, which are the initial words indicating punishment, as a reminder that whoever recites this surah, believes in it, and knows its realities, becomes safe from the seven levels of Hell." End of quote. What is in it is not hidden, and his answer neither benefits him nor suffices him. For someone may say: then let the *dhāl*, *wāw*, *nūn*, *ḥā'*, *ʿayn*, *mīm*, and *ghayn* be omitted as well, since the *wāw* is from *wayl* (woe), the *dhāl* from *dhilla* (humiliation), the *nūn* from *nār* (fire), the *ḥā'* from *ḥamīm* (boiling water), the *ʿayn* from *ʿadhāb* (punishment), the *mīm* from *mihād* (bed/resting place), and the *ghayn* from *ghawāshī* (overwhelming things). The verses are evident, and all of them concern the people of the Fire. The benefit of omitting these would be like the benefit of omitting those, without any difference at all. Moreover, in his words, may God Exalted have mercy on him, there is something other than this. Indeed, even granting that his statement is free from what has been said or may be said, I do not approve of it for Fakhr, who is the master who became the felicity of the religion, the proof of Islam, and the defender of its people.

As for attributing it to the Commander of the Faithful, ʿAlī, may God honour his face, when Caesar of Rome asked Muʿāwiya about this and he did not answer, so he asked ʿAlī and he answered: there is no basis for it. And even on the assumption of its acceptance, what was the Commander's purpose in being content with this measure, except to alert the questioner to secrets that are not hidden from you? So understand this, and may God Exalted take care of your guidance.

(Fifth, sixth, and seventh names): *al-Kanz* (the Treasure), *al-Wāfiyah* (the Sufficient), and *al-Kāfiyah* (the Adequate), because of what has been mentioned about its inclusion of hidden jewels; it suffices and is sufficient. Or because it is not halved in prayer, and nothing else can substitute for it in prayer.

(Eighth): *al-Asās* (the Foundation), because it is the origin of the Qur'an and the first surah in it.

(Ninth, tenth, eleventh, twelfth, and thirteenth): the Surah of Praise, the Surah of Gratitude, the Surah of Supplication, the Surah of Teaching the Request, and the Surah of Asking, because of its inclusion of these. As for its inclusion of praise, it is evident. Likewise gratitude, for whoever has been blessed by God with understanding. It is possible that these names are like "the Mother of the Qur'an" and "the Mother of the Book."

As for its inclusion of the third (ethics), it is like its inclusion of the first, rather more evident. As for teaching the request, it is because it begins with praise before it. The fifth is like the third, and these two are like those two, the third and fourth, as is not hidden.

(Fourteenth and fifteenth): the Surah of Intimate Conversation (*al-munājāh*) and the Surah of Delegation (*al-tafwīd*), because the servant converses with his Lord by saying: ﴿You alone we worship and You alone we ask for help﴾, and by this, delegation is achieved.

(Sixteenth, seventeenth, and eighteenth): the Incantation (*al-ruqyah*), the Cure (*al-shifā'*), and the Healing (*al-shāfiyah*). The authentic hadiths indicate this.

(Nineteenth): the Surah of Prayer, because it is obligatory or a pillar (*farīḍah*) in it. Recommendation is the view of some jurists, and a narration from some regarding voluntary prayer. It has been said: among its names is "the Prayer," based on the hadith: "I have divided the prayer between Me and My servant into two halves." He meant the surah. The linguistic metonymy, by the relation of the whole and the part, or of necessity, actually or by ruling, like the metonymy in ellipsis, is possible.

(Twentieth): *al-Nūr* (the Light), either because it is apparent through its frequent use, or because it illuminates hearts due to the greatness of its rank, or because what it contains of meanings is an expression of the light, meaning the Qur'an.

(Twenty-first): *al-Qur'ān al-ʿAẓīm* (the Great Qur'an), which is evident from what we have previously presented.

(Twenty-second): *al-Sabʿ al-Mathānī* (the Seven Oft-Repeated), because it consists of seven verses by consensus, and we have not seen anything sharing this except "Ara'ayta" (Surah al-Ma'un). The claim that it has eight verses is like the claim that it has nine; it is an anomalous view that does not deserve attention, or it is an error by a narrator. However, some counted the basmala as a verse but not "those upon whom You have bestowed favour," and some did the reverse, and the basis is the transmission. The second opinion is not weakened by the fact that the length of this verse does not correspond to the length of the verse-endings of other surahs. Moreover, in Surah al-Nasr there is something of this kind. It is repeated (*tuthannā*) and repeated (*tukarrar*) in every rak'ah and in every prayer containing bowing. Or the intended meaning is the common and usual meaning of prayer, so a single rak'ah is not objected to, nor is the funeral prayer. Moreover, there is disagreement concerning the *batīrā'* (a prayer without tashahhud), and the funeral prayer is a supplication, not a prayer in the true sense. It has been said that it is described by this because it is repeated (*tuthannā*) with another surah, or because it was revealed twice, or because it is of two kinds: supplication and praise, or because whenever the servant recites one verse of it, God repeats it by reporting His action, as in the well-known hadith. Other statements have also been made. These statements are based on the assumption that *mathānī* comes from *tathniyah* (repetition). It is possible that it comes from *thanā'* (praise), because it contains praise of God, or because of what is reported of praise for whoever recites it. It is also possible that it comes from *thunyā* (exception), because God has singled it out for this Community, and to God belongs praise for this blessing.

Then, the wisdom in the Qur'an being divided into surahs, like books, contrary to al-Zarkashi's view, is that it is more energizing for the reciter and more motivating for acquiring knowledge, like the traveller who, when he covers a mile or a league, refreshes himself by it and becomes energetic for the journey. When the memorizer takes a surah, he believes he has taken from the Book of God a distinct portion, and so what he has memorized becomes great in his eyes. Also, when a genus includes various types and kinds, it is better than if it had only one chapter beneath it. Along with this, there is in it a confirmation that the surah by itself is a miracle and one of the signs of God, Exalted is He. The wisdom in its being long and short is more evident than to be hidden.
